speechtext:
Perhaps the
lion, member will allow me at this point to read the following communication from the Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe):
To supplement the accompanying memorandum from the Commissioner of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police, I wish to say that Mr. Anderson is acting usually as legal agent for the government at Regina. He has always done so satisfactorily and there was no reason or justification to remove the legal work from his hands.

The point of the whole
matter is this-

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Perhaps my hon. friend will allow me one question so that the record may be complete. He has referred to Mr. Bryant, K.C., 4 p.m. and he has also mentioned another gentleman as holding a particular office. Is it not true that Mr. Bryant is the president of the Conservative Association of Regina and was a Conservative candidate in the last provincial election?

That may be true. I do
not know but we will assume it is; I have no idea.
Oh, oh.

I do not see the reason for the hilarious roar from hon. gentlemen opposite. When has it been an offence for a citizen to be a member of a Conservative association, and a great virtue for a man to be secretary of a Liberal association. My point to the Prime Minister, Mr. Speaker, is that a case involving the most intimate and intricate police investigation was given in good faith to the department with all the confidential information; the mounted police went about their duty properly; they had to keep the thing secret. Mr. Bryant happened to be the one who knew something about it, and the operative retained Mr. Bryant to guide him in the prosecution of that case. When they succeeded in apprehending some of the offenders suddenly action was stayed and there was a change in the counsel. Why? It was for purely political purposes.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: I submit that the statement of Commissioner Starnes is emphatically in contradiction with what my hon. friend has just said.

Commissioner Starnes knew nothing about the retention of Mr. Anderson until he was instructed by his minister to make the change. The point is that all through these investigations one thing has been constantly brought to the attention of the people of Canada, and to put it mildly they are exceedingly impatient with the practice. Wherever responsible officers of the department seemed to be doing their duty there would appear on the scene, through some subterranean method, individuals with influence who would interfere -with the proper prosecution of those duties.
Take the Cohen case which I have already cited. Cohen was under surveillance for a considerable time; Officers Knox and Duncan, who have been carrying on investigations in different parts of the country but perhaps particularly in the great centre of Montreal, caught Cohen red-handed in four or five seizures. There are still three or four cases out against him and yet this case has been fiddled along through the courts, and there is ample evidence to show that it was political influence from members of the House which prevented the case from going forward. What happened? The case was set for hearing a few days ago, before the close of the spring assizes. Then this frame-up occurred, absolutely without the knowledge of departmental officials; they were not consulted at all. In the evidence before the House at the present moment is a statement or a precis showing clearly that this same man, Benjamin Cohen, sought to have this delay brought about by the excuse that he could1 give information regarding others. And why did he do this? He did it simply because the ablest lawyers in Montreal realized that they could'not keep him out of gaol. The stay in proceedings, forsooth, is made because this notorious silk smuggler, Cohen, must not go to gaol; there is no other reason for the sudden interference, towards the end of the assizes, when they had exhausted every measure of chicanery to defeat the courts. There is no other excuse than that the present Minister of Customs (Mr. Boivin) arranged through the Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe) for the mounted police to step in and interfere with the procedure in this case.

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Absolutely untrue.

My only answer to the Minister of Justice is that three times dur-

Customs Inquiry-Mr. Stevens
ing the course of my speech of February 2 he rose in his place and absolutely denied all knowledge of the matters which later came before the committee, and there is ample evidence on the files and records to show that the minister knew all about it.

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Still untrue.

I attach to the minister's statement to-day exactly the same weight which the evidence shows to be merited in the previous case.
Some one asks me about the Aziz case; I will not deal with that. The hon. member for West Hamilton (Mr. Bell) will take up that case, and I do not intend to trespass on his time.

Before the hon. gentleman
passes to another point, will he tell me whether these two cases which he has just mentioned were brought to the attention of the committee?

The Cohen case was set
out in full before the committee; the precis is on file. I cannot give the hon. gentleman the pages, but there are probably almost twenty pages of evidence in connection with that case. It was not brought before the committee for trial because it was then in the courts, and that is one of the reasons, Mr. Speaker, why I feel so intensely about this interference. Just as I said a short time ago, it presages that in the future the same influences and the same practices which have brought about the debauchery and collapse of this department will be carried on.
Will the hon. gentleman tell me whether the Regina case was brought before the committee?

No. I told the House a moment ago, and I also stated in my letter to the Prime Minister, that inasmuch as it required intimate and secret police work in order to be successful I thought it unwise to bring the matter before the committee. I gave it in confidence to the officers of the department and again I say that Mr. Taylor, now in charge of the department, acted in this matter in a most exemplary way; I have no fault to find whatever. It was not until from the Justice department political influence interfered that anything went wrong in connection with that case.
In the preparation of this report consideration was given to the responsibility of the present minister and his colleagues in regard to certain cases in the direction of which he allowed himself to be influenced by political pressure and political expediency involving

serious violation of the principles of the inviolability of the courts. Consideration was also given to the conduct of several members whose alleged importunity influenced the minister to give partial attention to particular cases. Upon these points, Mr. Speaker, the committee could not agree. The hon. member for Peace River (Mr. Kennedy) refused to support a motion to report censure of the minister, and in a substitute motion restricted the action of the committee to a mere reference of the evidence to the House. As the hon. member had the deciding vote, and the Liberal members rejected both motions, it prevented the incorporation of either motion in the report. I merely make this statement in explanation of the absence of any such reference in the report.
I hope the House appreciates the fact that this report is an intensely important document; it contains a great deal of valuable constructive matter, and it also lays upon the administration certain grave duties. The question before the House is not so much if you approve of the general terms of the report, but rather if this report is a good one -as it is generally admitted to be-can this administration be entrusted with the duty of carrying out the terms of the report? And now I have an amendment to move, Mr. Speaker, which I will read, but before doing 30, Mr. Speaker, I might say that it is realiy a composite amendment made up of the two that were proposed to the committee. I move, seconded by the hon. member for Kent (Mr. Doucet):
That the report ibe not now adopted, buit that it be referred back to the special committee with instructions to add thereto the following clauses as sub-clauses to paragraph six:
"The evidence further discloses that ministerial action has been influenced by the improper pressure of political associates and friends of the minister, or acting minister, administering the department, resulting in the suspension and in some instances the abandonment of prosecutions against those charged with violation of the statutes, and in the loss of revenue to the country. Moreover, successful appeals have been made to the minister and acting minister administering the department to improperly interfere with the course [DOT]of justice between the conviction of the offenders and the execution of judgment thereon. The Prime Minister and the government had knowledge for some considerable time of the rapid degeneration of the Department of Customs and Excise, and their failure to take prompt and effective remedial action is wholly indefensible. The conduct of the present minister of the department, the Hon. George H. Boivin, in the case [DOT]of Moses Aziz, is utterly unjustifiable.
"Your committee deplores the practice, as Tevealed by the evidence, of certain men influential in public life to direct appeals, to the minister to relax and depart from the proper administration of his department for reasons of political expediency.
"Your committee is of the opinion that this practice is detrimental to the best interests of the country and

Customs Inquiry-Mr. Boivin
prejudicial to the administration of the department.
"And that the committee for such purpose be revived."
Hon. GEORGE H. BOIVIN (Minister of Customs and Excise): Mr. Speaker, upon one ground at least I am in perfect accord with the hon. member for Vancouver Centre (Mr. Stevens), and that is in expressing my thanks, the thanks of this House of Commons and, I am sure, of the people of Canada to the members of the Customs committee, without distinction of political party, for the strenuous labours that they have performed, for the close attention that they have given to their duties, and for the fairly comprehensive report which they have presented to this House this afternoon. I agree still more heartily with him in his remarks concerning the work performed upon that committee by the chairman of the committee, our good friend from St. Henri (Mr. Mercier), who presided over all of its sessions, and who certainly displayed a spirit of fairness and impartiality which had a great deal to do, I am sure, with removing the political passion and prejudice that may have been apparent during the first few meetings of the committee.
I am not prepared to go quite the same distance with my hon. friend from Vancouver Centre in saying that I agree entirely with every word that the report contains, but speaking as a member of the government, and also speaking personally as Minister of Customs and Excise, I will say that every recommendation contained in that report if it is approved and adopted will be carried out to the letter so far as it is possible to do so. I regret, for instance, to see in the report among those who are recommended for retirement the name of Mr. Henry McLaughlin, surveyor of customs and excise for the port of Montreal. It is not my duty to defend Mr. McLaughlin before this House, I do not propose to do so, but as I have received a letter from him to-day, I merely ask to place it on record in order that if by any chance the amendment is carried and the report is referred back to the committee that they may consider the contents of this letter during their special session. The letter reads as follows: Hon. George H. Boivin,
Minister of Customs an4 Excise,
Ottawa.
I hate very much to trouble you at this time, but I feel very keenly the manner in which they propose to retire me. I have not been called before the committee to answer any charge, consequently I am unaware of having done anything that would call for a deoision such as the committee has rendered.
As regards the liquor samples referred to in Mr. Duncan's report, I wish to state positively that I have not received a single liquor sample during the past six
years. Before that Mr. Cote and Mr. Corbeil were in the habit of distributing before Christmas a few liquor samples to the employees.
Any orders issued by me to the officers at distilleries and other plants were always authorized by the department, otherwise I would not have issued them.
I feel that I have your entire sympathy and would like very much to retire under different circumstances, as I certainly have no objections to retiring but would like to do so of my own volition.
Yours very truly,
Heney McLaughlin,
Surveyor of Customs-Excise.
I merely place the letter on Hansard in order, as I said before, that it may be considered by the committee if by any chance they re-convene to discuss the amendment which has been submitted to the House by the hon. member for Vancouver Centre today.
The hon. member for Vancouver Centre prided himself on placing me in contradiction with some of the remarks I made on the second day of February last in answer to his unexpected charges. He has built up a very vociferous ease against me by saying that I had misled the House when I pretended that the alcohol sold to the Dominion Distillery Products Limited was for blending purposes instead of denaturing purposes. That, apparently, is the only contradiction which he has so far found in my remarks. That is the only falsehood I addressed to the House of Commons when I spoke on that famous night of February 2, 1926. My hon. friend, I think, will do me the justice of saying that on that occasion I spoke without preparation, without notes, without investigation. Mjy hon. friend took the trouble on two different occasions since the opening of this House to rise and make a special request to you, Mr. Speaker, to pass to the order of motions, to withdraw two or three motions standing in his name on the order paper, but it was without any notice that he withdrew his original motion from the order paper in order to take this party by surprise on that famous night. My hon. friend may shake his head, but I defy him to rise in his place and say that' it was not to the Clerk rather than to the House that he addressed himself in order to have his original motion withdrawn from the order paper, knowing well that while that motion was on the order paper he could not take this party by surprise, and that would have to be withdrawn before he could bring in his amendment to the motion made by the Minister of Justice.

That is nonsense.
Customs Inquiry-Mr. Boivin

That night I did say that
I had sold to a personal friend, W. J. Hushion, fifteen thousand and some odd gallons of alcohol which had been stored on the barge Tremblay. Let me tell my hon. friend, and he knows it very well, that one of the reasons why the attack was made upon W. J. Hushion was because he was a former Liberal member of the House of Commons. That is where I formed my friendship with that gentleman; and I assert now, as I asserted then, that when Mr. Hushion spoke to me for the first time about purchasing alcohol, it was a revelation to me to know that he was interested in any way in the Dominion Distillers Products Limited. I ascertained it then for the first time. I went to an officer of the department to whom my good friend the hon. member for Vancouver Centre has just paid such a high tribute of praise, Mr, G. W. Taylor. He is 'acting deputy minister now but at that time was assistant deputy minister and chief of the Excise branch in the Department of Customs and Excise. I asked Mr. Taylor if we had a right to sell the alcohol. He told me that we had and he has so sworn before the committee. I asked him what would be a reasonable rate for the alcohol. He told me that he would look up and ascertain the highest rate at which alcohol was ever sold to a distillery. He examined the records. We had an offer of 35 cents, an offer made by the same corporation, in the office of Mr. Wilson in the department, but which had not been reported to the deputy minister, which had not been reported to the chief of the Excise branch, and which had not been reported to the minister. It was ascertained that on one occasion alcohol of that kind had been sold for 35J cents, and it was for that reason that I told Mr. Hushion by long distance telephone that he could not get the alcohol for less than 36 cents a gallon. I said that he was in a hurry to get it but my hon. friend pretends that could not be because he had bought 60,000 gallons elsewhere. My hon. friend admits that the Dominion Distillers had bought 60,000 gallons elsewhere for 38 cents a gallon, or two cents more per gallon than the alcohol sold by the government. My hon. friend and his papers throughout Canada have tried to make out that this government lost over $800,000 by the sale of that alcohol when he admits himself that there was a difference of two cents a gallon between the price paid to the government and the price that would have to be paid to other distillers in order to buy it from them. My hon. friend knows well that this alcohol could not have been sold with excise duty unless it was sold for potable purposes. fMr. Stevens.]
Which it was.

My hon. friend now says
"which it was." My hon. friend just said a few minutes ago, and I defy him to deny it, that this alcohol was No. 1 P denatured alcohol exported from Canada under bond,, with the exception of three cars which were possibly not exported from this country. If there were three cars of alcohol not exported from Canada I want to say that the Minister of Customs and Excise or the Department of Customs and Excise at that time knew nothing about it. I want to say that every carload was shipped from the distillery under a bond that it would be exported from Canada and that not one of these bonds was released until the B-13 or the export entries signed by the officer at the border were returned to the department. That is the precaution which was used to make sure that No. 1-F denatured alcohol would not be sold here in Canada. My hon. friend knows that no distillery would pay excise on alcohol when it goes into the distillery. The excise on alcohol is paid when the alcohol comes out, and I stated the other night, and I repeat now, that not one ounce, not one bottle, not one gallon of that alcohol could have left that distillery for potable purposes without the payment of excise duty on it, and when it did leave the distillery without the payment of excise, it left in tin cans labelled "poison" on its way to the United States, not for potable purposes, but as No. 1-F denatured alcohol, as the hon. member says himself, for rubbing and medicinal purposes.
Contrary to the regulations.

My hon. friend says, "but
once before alcohol was sold at fifteen dollars and some cents a gallon." Alcohol was once sold to the Quebec Liquor Commission, good alcohol which had been seized.

Precisely the same as
this.

How can my hon. friend
make that assertion?
Because it is in evidence.

I thought my hon. friend
would make that statement, and that is why I want to read a letter from the Quebec Liquor Commission. Why, all through this inquiry it has been said that the minister was not trying to do his duty, that he was trying to favour a political friend, that if this liquor had only been sold to the Quebec Liquor Commission we could have got our excise upon it. I hold in my hand a letter signed by the

Customs Inquiry-Mr. Boivin
deputy chairman of the Quebec Liquor Commission, written to my much despised predecessor on the 29th January, 1925, stating that they would not buy that alcohol because it was not fit for human consumption.
Will the minister explain why that letter was not put in evidence and the witness produced for examination?
Order, order.

The Prime Minister and
other hon. members interrupted. Take your medicine.

I think the question asked
by the right hon. leader of the opposition is a fair one. He wishes to know why this letter was not produced before the committee. Because the hon. member who received this letter was not called before the committee and also because the letter was never addressed to the department. If it had been addressed to the department it would undoubtedly be on the departmental files, but it was addressed to the Hon. Jacques Bureau when he was at home at Trois-Rivieres, undoubtedly detained there through illness. My hon. friends smile, sneer and laugh-the same hon. members who allowed Hon. Jacques Bureau to put through his estimates year after year without a single dissenting voice; the same hon. gentlemen who were willing then and there to accept his favours. All of them* are not here but many of them are present, and they are going to sneer because I said that during the past year the hon. senator had been ill and unable to attend to his departmental duties. It was a secret from no one.
Nobody sneered at that.

I think the minister is quite
out of order; nobody sneered. The minister should calm himself.
Perhaps my good friend the right hon. leader of the opposition will tell us what the hon. members sneered at?

I will tell him what I
smiled at. It was the suggestion of the minister that because the letter was received by Mr. Bureau it could not go into evidence.
What is the date?

January 29, 1925. That I think disposes of at least one accusation-T- the accusation levelled against the minister of trying to favour a political friend and endeavouring to divert revenue from the public treasury.
Referring to the statement of my hon. friend from Vancouver Centre, I would like to disprove at once the claims that a great deal of the alcohol thus denatured was not shipped out of the country. He has read a letter, for which he says I am responsible, written by the acting deputy minister, the existence of which letter, he says, the minister well knew on the second February. I never saw the letter and my hon. friend knows that I never saw it. It was written by the chief of the Excise department to the Dominion Distillers giving them the same specific instructions concerning the shipment of denatured alcohol as have always been given to every distillery in the country including some of those old reliable distilleries who happen to have Conservative owners whom my hon. friend does not wish to blame or to hold up to censure. The instructions given to the distilleries are absolutely the same, and the letter sent to the Dominion Distillers on this occasion was exactly the same as the others.
If it is true that the Dominion Distillers succeeded in evading the law; if it is true that two or three carloads of that denatured alcohol did not reach the United States; if it is true that it was sold in Canada and that is not proven, it is due to one of two things. Either the bond for export has not been re-

leased and the export entry has not been returned, or some dishonest official on the border has signed a false export entry and returned it to the department without exporting the liquor. One or the other is the case. Is the minister to be held responsible for that? When I find employees on the border not living up to the liquor regulations of this country, not living up to the rules prescribed for the export of liquor from this country, those employees will be punished and dismissed. One of those employees from a port not far from Windsor is now under suspension for having acted as a distiller's agent, and there is a member sitting on the other side of the House, who will vote in favour of this amendment, who has come to my office in this building twice asking me to reinstate this man.
Does the minister not know that this alcohol No. 1-F special is not admissible to the United States?
I will say to my hon. friend that no alcoholic liquor of any kind is admissible to the United States.

My hon. friend has
missed the point of my question. He argues that this alcohol was sold as denatured alcohol for export, not as potable alcohol. Denatured alcohol of certain classes is not prohibited in the United States, but this class of denatured alcohol is prohibited because it can easily be converted into potable alcohol, according to the evidence and according to the United States regulations.

I agree with my hon. friend to a certain extent. I do not know why he rose the second time to interrupt me. In answer to his question whether I knew that this alcohol No. 1-F special is not admissible to the United States, I said that all alcoholic liquor is contraband in the United States.
That is not my point.

I say that rye, Scotch, gin
and beer are contraband in the United States, and still they are being sent there by the boat load every day to the knowledge of my hon. friends opposite, of hon. members on this side of the House, of the Department of Customs and of the United States government, who are advised of every shipload that leaves Windsor for any point in the United States. Every boatload of liquor that is loaded at any one of the border points is given a clearance only when notice of that clearance has been given to a United States officer on the other side of the boundary line. It is true that those boats may never go to the ports to

Customs Inquiry-Mr. Boivin
which they are destined. It is impossible for us to follow them or to determine exactly where they are going.
I agree entirely with my hon. friend and with the recommendations of the report that closer and more stringent regulations must be made concerning the export of liquor from Canada to the nation termed by my hon. friend, "a friendly nation to the south of us." But what I want my hon. friend to admiG-and I know he will be fair enough to admit it-that up to the present time and especially since I took charge of the department, we have been living up to the rules and regulations of the treaty made between Canada and the United States of America. My hon. friend may well shake his head, but since I entered the department instructions have been given that there will be no camouflage bills of lading. For five or six days the export of liquor was practically paralyzed by a ruling given by the department that shipments of liquor would not be given clearance to Mexico or other points that could not be reached by the Great Lakes; that those camouflaged bills of lading would no longer be accepted; that it is absolutely necessary to show at the inland point from which the liquor was being shipped that it was being shipped from Windsor or some other point for export from Canada and that it must be accompanied by the export entry showing its destination in the United States. We have lived up in every respect to the treaty made between this country and the United States.
What I say-and I have been led away, by the question asked by my hon. friend- is that this No. 1-F denatured alcohol is in absolutely the same position as other alcohol shipped from Canada to the United States. It was shipped with an export entry; the bond given for its shipment was released only when the export entry was returned to the department, and therefore I say that not one dollar of revenue has been lost in favouritism to the Dominion Distillery Products Company Limited, or any other distiller in Canada.
There is one other point I want to make. My hon. friend says that I am not qualified to collect the accounts that may be due to the Department of Customs and Excise by some of the people who are brought before the committee, because I live in and represent a constituency not far from Rock Island, Que. My hon. friend will at least, I hope, admit that my constituency is not contiguous to that of Stanstead. But even if it were, even if I represented the constituency of Stanstead itself and even although the task might be a disagreeable one, I think I would be still
qualified to order a competent attorney to take the necessary legal proceedings against any persons who have defrauded the Dominion government.
The hon. member says that the minister admitted in his speech some months ago that he was a friend of Mr. Alfred Bissonnette I admitted it some months ago. I was his friend; I have been his friend for several years. He represents the county of Stanstead in the Quebec legislature; I represent the county of Shefford in the Dominion parliament. We have been out on many a political campaign together. But it was not until after this inquiry started that I knew that he had any interest whatever in the Peerless Overall Company or that I even knew that he was interested in the sale of overalls. I knew him as a politician and as a friend. The statement I made the other night I repeat, and I have nothing to retract in that connection.
There is, it is true, one more charge against me, a charge of such grave consequence that by it not only myself but the entire government of which I am a member must totter and fall. What is that charge? My hon. friend has left to a special pleader the task of arraigning me upon it before this jury of the House of Commons. That charge is that I consented to listen to the representations of a member of parliament before I would order the issue of a warrant of commitment against a man who had been accused and convicted of having smuggled liquor in his possession. That is the charge; but I ask the House to be good enough to go into the details of it and see to what extent I am guilty. To read the newspapers published under the direction of hon. gentlemen opposite one would almost conclude that I had gone to the province of New Brunswick and argued and pleaded with a judge not to incarcerate this man, Moses Aziz. Let me however tell the House what actually happened.
Moses Aziz was found guilty on the 18th day of August, 1925, three weeks before I even surmised that I would ever be appointed Minister of Customs. At the time that sentence was rendered I had no idea whatever that I might be Minister of Customs on September 5 following. No request had come to me, and I had no knowledge either of the case itself or even of the existence of Aziz until the second day I was in my office. Sitting at my desk in Ottawa, on or about September 28, I was approached by my secretary who had several hundred letters to dispose of,-the accumulation of a month. He was trying as rapidly as possible to deal with them, and reading this one to me he remarked, "This is a request from Mr. Robichaud, the member for
Customs Inquiry-Mr. Boivin

Gloucester, asking you to withhold a warrant of commitment against a man who was arrested down there for having smuggled goods in his possession." Having absolutely no experience and no knowledge of the laws of New Brunswick my first step was to call in the deputy minister and inquire of him whether we had the power to withhold execution of the sentence until such time as the member could make whatever representations he had to offer.
I was in a hurry to return home, having attended a meeting of council that day. It was during the election campaign and I had been in the Eastern Townships for several days. I had come to Ottawa on a hurried visit and was endeavouring as far as possible to relieve the burdens of my colleague sitting to my left who had continued to act as Minister of Customs and Excise. Because of that desire to relieve him so far as I could, I went to the department and looked into the correspondence with my secretary. When Mr. Farrow, the deputy minister, was called in, he not only declared that we had the right to do as requested but, he added, 5 p.m. "There is a letter on the file from the chief of the Remission branch in the Department of Justice in which the statement is made that the Department of Justice cannot deal with the case, but that the Minister of Customs has a perfect right to dispose of it as he sees fit." That letter, signed by Mr. Gallagher, will be found on the files, having been produced in evidence before the committee.
Now what are the facts? Why did the minister, even at that late date, consider it advisable to hear the member representing the constituency before this man was sent to gaol? There were several reasons. A letter from Mr. Stewart, the customs preventive officer at that point, which unfortunately was not filed, but which I have here, shows that Moses Aziz had turned King's evidence and had convicted his own brother and another person of smuggling. That evidence was given in a New Brunswick court on the same day as Aziz himself was convicted, and there was a promise from this Mr. Stewart, a veiled promise, an uncertain promise, if you like, that instead of being prosecuted for an indictable offence under section 219, Aziz would be prosecuted summarily. And that conveyed to him the impression that he would be relieved of a gaol sentence. That is one point. The next point is this: there is an assertion in the record, it - is read into the record in a letter from Mr. Veniot, that the smuggling operation complained of took place before the twenty-seventh day of June, 1925,

the date upon which the new law was adopted. Previous to that date no gaol punishment was obligatory, and the smuggling in this case had actually taken place before the new law went into force. But it was because Aziz happened still to have the goods in his possession, not having disposed of them in the interval, that he was sentenced to imprisonment. The law, however, provides for imprisonment for a term of one year, and he was sentenced to three months' imprisonment only. The judge therefore must himself have made a mistake; evidently he had doubts about his right to send the man to prison, because he sentenced him to a period of three months. There was a promise, in the form of a telegram from my predecessor to Mr. Veniot, to the effect that a revaluation of the liquor would be made, which revaluation had not taken place. These were the facts I had before me and I had no knowledge whatever of the practice in New Brunswick. I have since ascertained that the custom in New Brunswick is that after a man is condemned and after sentence has been passed upon him, it is incumbent upon the private prosecutor to go to the court and solicit the issue of a warrant of commitment which he hands to the gaoler in order that the convicted person may be apprehended and lodged in gaol. That is not the custom in my province but, I am informed that is the practice followed in New Brunswick. Now, the Minister of Customs, who in this instance was acting in the capacity of prosecutor, did not make any request of the judge to withhold sentence. He did not make any request of the sheriff to stay the execution of his writ. The Minister of Customs merely carried out his duties as he had a right to do, giving notice to his own officer in the province of New Brunswick that this man was not to be incarcerated until Mr. Robichaud, the member representing the constituency, could come to Ottawa and confer with the minister. Was there any intent on the part of the minister to keep the man out of gaol? Do my hon. friends believe that was the intent? Some smile now, although some do not. Some of them are going to vote against the Minister of Customs in this case with a great deal of regret. More than one of them will rise in his place and vote through party allegiance.
So far as the first statement is concerned, all who vote against the minister will vote with regret.

I thank my right hon.
friend for that statement, and I believe it. I believe the right hon. gentleman would

Customs Inquiry-Mr. Boivin
crucify his own brother with regret but he would do it in order to serve the Conservative party. I would that it were possible for every hon. member to vote according to his own wish and his own opinion; I am quite willing to leave my case in the hands of this honourable House if hon. members are not obliged to follow party ties. Is it a crime for a minister of the crown to say to a member of parliament, "I will wait until I hear you."
Precious help in election.

I told my hon. friend five minutes ago that I had not seen the letter at the time the request was granted; the request was transmitted to me in a very hurried way by my secretarjq sitting on the other side of the desk. But I say now that if I had seen the request and been cognizant of all the other circumstances my conduct would have been the same; I will say further that if this request had come to me from a Conservative member of parliament, my conduct and my reply would have been absolutely the same.
As I said a moment, ago, I had no intention of keeping this man out of gaol if he were guilty; on the other hand, I had no intention of letting him go to gaol if I could help it if, on the merits of the case, he did not deserve to go to gaol. That will be made very clear by reference to page 1324 of the evidence, where you will find the letter written by the minister to Mr. Robichaud on November IS, 1925, two weeks after I took possession of my desk. I said:
I have before me a memorandum concerning the case of Mr. Moses Aziz, who was condemned by the court *to a fine of $150 and to three months' imprisonment Tor having had liquor in his possession.
The fine of $150 was paid, but the execution of the warrant of commitment was temporarily suspended.
I have examined the case with care, and I can find ho reason for which the imposed sentence should not "be executed, but I will keep the matter in suspense *Until I get a reply from you, in the event of your *having other representations to make to me.
The officers of the department contend that the efforts made to prevent smuggling of liquors will be much lessened if this man is let go without further punishment.
Yours very devotedly,
Geo. H. Boivin.
I think it only fair to the hon. member for Gloucester (Mr. Robichaud) to say that he immediately answered this letter, and under date of November 25, wrote as follows: Honourable and Dear Sir,
Referring to your favour of November 18, on the subject of penalties imposed on Mr. Moses Aziz, for having had liquors in his possession, will you please do 14011-307
your best to suspend all proceedings until I see you *when I return to Ottawa.
With an expression of my best sentiments,
Yours truly,
(Signed) J. G. Robichaud,
*	Member for Gloucester.
Hon. members should remember that it was then pretty well decided that the House should meet on December 10, so the delay asked for was not long. It was after this date that the papers throughout the length and breadth of Canada carried a notice that my good friend from Vancouver Centre (Mr. Stevens) intended to demand a parliamentary inquiry to probe into the most hidden recesses of the administration of the Department of Customs and Excise. This case was on my desk awaiting consideration. It is true that after this notice had been given I could have called Mr. Robichaud and said, "I am scared; here is a parliamentary inquiry coming on. This man Aziz must get into gaol before they are able to reach his case, so we will be able to save ourselves from criticism." But that is not the conduct I wanted to follow; I wanted to place the record before the committee in the same condition as it was at the time notice was given that such a committee would be constituted, in order that the Department of Customs and Excise might be judged upon its merits and that the minister might be judged according to the crime he had committed.
I think I gave all the extenuating circumstances in connection with the matter when I referred to the fact that the liquor had been imported before the new law came into force; that under the new law, the sentence could not have been for three months; that a revaluation of the liquor had been promised, but had not been made, and hon. members should not forget that Mr. Moses Aziz was not entirely unpunished. He had already paid a fine of $150 and costs of $38, and his liquor had been confiscated. The Minister of Customs had not withdrawn the warrant of commitment, nor had it been annulled; the minister had not given a pardon to Mr. Moses Aziz, but was merely awaiting the further representations of Mr. Robichaud. The proof of that statement lies in the fact that Mr. Moses Aziz is now in gaol, serving his sentence. After the matter had been considered by the committee, after I had given my evidence before the committee and the facts were made known, then and only then did I carry out the suggestion of the hon. member for Vancouver Centre, that Moses Aziz be sent to gaol at once. Then I gave instructions through Mr. Wilson, the chief preventive officer, to send Moses Aziz to gaol.



Customs Inquiry-Mr. Boivin

When did you
see Mr. Robichaud?

On the morning following
my evidence before the Customs committee I met Mr. Robichaud and talked with him in the rotunda opposite this door. I asked him for his additional reasons, if he had any to give me, and Mr. Robichaud said that unfortunately he had no reasons other than those which were already on file, but that he thought those were sufficient. He had given several other reasons concerning the condition of the man's family and the necessity that he be free to provide for them. I spoke with him the morning after I gave my evidence before the committee, twelve hours before I gave instructions to Mr. Wilson to have Mr. Aziz incarcerated.

Before the minister passes on, in order that we may be absolutely clear, do I understand that the minister had not himself actually read the text of Mr. Robichaud's letter when he came to his decision in the matter?

What is the date
of that?

June 7, 1926. That is the opinion of the Deputy Minister of Justice, based upon the law which I have just cited, which is section 266 of the Customs Act; so it is plain, I think, that the minister had the right to act.
Whether it was expedient for the minister to do what he did may be open to question. It may be that owing to the terms of that letter, written by an hon. member and for which I am not responsible-I think the greatest mistake I ever committed in connection with the whole matter was the placing of this letter on the file and bringing it before the committee, when it was marked "private and confidential," but it was done merely for the purpose of showing to the committee that we had nothing to hide, that every document and every letter in connection with the entire case would be placed before them and be entirely at their disposal-it was inexpedient to grant the request, but there is one fact that must be remembered, and that is that the mistake, if any, consists in having delayed the execution of a three months' sentence. There was no pardon granted. Execution was delayed at the
request of a member of parliament who had certain representations to make. I have stated before, and I state again, that if that request had come from a Conservative member of parliament it would have been granted in absolutely the same way. That member would have been heard and the case would have been judged on its merits, in so far as the minister has the right to judge, in so far as the minister has the authority to intervene.
I am informed by the best authorities in the Department of Justice that I only exercised the authority which I had, and after having given the case consideration, after having kept it in absolutely the same position in which it was, to submit it to the Customs inquiry, the case has now been carried to a conclusion and the warrant of commitment has been issued.
Those are the two charges levelled against the minister. I hope that when hon. members come to cast their vote, be it late to-night or some time to-morrow, they will bear in mind the explanation that I have frankly and clearly given, and that they will not be misled by the statement that perhaps will be made by the hon. member who I know, very reluctantly, will bring this case before parliament, and who will endeavour to base his case possibly on the evidence given by the minister himself before the committee. It is true that I said when I was called before that committee, "I may have been wrong in doing this." I had not gone into the details of the case. I had not got this opinion from the Deputy Minister of Justice. I had not gone thoroughly through the record, as I have done since. I placed the case in its true position before the committee, and the hon. member for West Calgary, who has the reputation at least of being a very eminent barrister and counsel, stated that I had done wrong. When he was asking me the different questions, and I was volunteering my evidence, I said, "Yes, perhaps I have, but if I have, those are the facts and that is the extent of my crime."
There is one point right here I wish to bring before the public in the galleries and the people of Canada, and I hope it will be mentioned in the press: In spite of all that this inquiry has delved into and worked over for a period of four and a half months in an endeavour to find something with which they could blacken this government, with which they could blacken the reputation not only of my predecessor but of the acting minister, and even of the Prime Minister and the Minister of Justice, there is one thing which shines out above all others, and that is that

Customs Inquiry-Mr. Boivin
there is not one important official in the Department of Customs, and there is not one minister or acting minister, past or present, who can be accused of having accepted any bribe to interfere with the proper execution of his duties. You may accuse the Hon. Jacques Bureau of having had a great big generous heart; you may accuse him of having been kind and good to his political friends and to his political foes, you may accuse him of having erred on the side of leniency in connection with the punishment of offenders, you may accuse him of having had a little too much confidence in some of his officials in the port of Montreal or elsewhere, but you cannot point a finger to where Jacques Bureau accepted a dollar as a bribe. Neither can you level such an accusation against the Acting Minister of Customs nor at the minister who is now in charge of that department. My opinion of the mentality of the people of Canada is that when a minister gives to the service of his country the best that is in him, when that minister is free from graft and free from corruption, when it is proven that neither he nor his subordinates have been influenced by paltry contributions or gifts of any kind, when it is proven that they have attempted to carry out their duties honestly, and that the only accusation that can be brought against them is that of having been a little too lenient and too generous the offence will be easily forgiven.
The inquiry has consumed four and a half months. I do not want the hon. member for Vancouver Centre or the hon. member for West Hamilton (Mr. Bell)) to think for a moment that in my opinion it has not been of any use w'hatever to Canada. I did say on a public platform in the early days of the inquiry, when there was a great deal of political squabbling, that I feared it would cost an enormous amount of money, and that the money would be entirely wasted. But I am ready and willing to admit that when I made that statement I made it conditional upon the fact that it would be carried on as it was then. I want to make the statement now and give credit to the members of the committee-and I want my hon. friend the member for Vancouver Centre to appropriate whatever credit he desires for himself-that I think the Customs inquiry has done a great good to this Dominion and to the Department of Customs and Excise. It has been of great assistance to the present minister and will be helpful to the minister who will succeed me in carrying on these duties and in preventing smuggling. I want also to pay a tribute to Mr. Sparks of the Commercial Protective Association, with whom I had some misun-
del-standing at the beginning of the inquiry. In my original speech in this House I blamed Mr. Sparks, and I blame him still for the fact that having got information from employees of my own department, he carried it to Mr. Stevens instead of bringing it to the Minister of Customs and Excise. I blamed him for it at that time and I blame him for it to-day; but I will say that the most instructive part of the entire evidence is undoubtedly the recommendations made by that same Commercial Protective Association. I want to give the association due credit for that. I have read these recommendations very carefully. Many of them are very valuable. In my humble judgment they are the most valuable representations made before the committee; and I want to say if I remain in the department as minister I will not only endeavour to carry out the recommendations of the report itself but I will also read in conjunction with it the suggestions made to the committee by the Commercial Protective Association.
There are many other things which I think my hon. friend will admit. One of the things I would like to have him admit is that for the first two and a half months of this inquiry every jot and tittle of evidence adduced before the committee was taken from a report which had already been prepared at the request of the Minister of Customs and Excise by an employee of the government and laid upon the table for the information of members of the committee.
My hon. friends may say: "It is because notice of a motion for an inquiry was given in the press that you gentlemen of the Liberal party hurried to have this investigation made." Now, it is stated clearly in the evidence by no less a personage than Inspector Duncan himself that the arrangements were all made with the Minister of Customs and Excise, that he was on his way to Montreal on November 27, 1925 to start his investigation, and that it was not until the 1st December, or four days later, that we received the first intimation in the press that the hon. member for Vancouver Centre had any idea of moving for a committee of investigation. As soon as I took over the department, after the elections, acting with the consent of the Prime Minister, acting in close co-operation with my good friend the Minister of Finance, who had unlimited confidence in the private investigator of that department, we secured the services of Mr. Duncan. He was sent to Montreal and on December 10th, long before this inquiry ever started, Mr. Bisaillon, who is the man against whom the hon. member for Vancouver

Customs Inquiry-Mr. Botvin
Centre directed most of his thunder in his speech on February 2, had been dismissed from the service. I think for at least three weeks the committee probed andi investigated to determine for their owa satisfaction that the Department of Customs and Excise was perfectly justified in dismissing Mr. Bisaillon.
I may say that Mr. Bisaillon was a very able witness, and the committee came very near not being able to prove that the department was justified, but ultimately they succeeded in doing so.
Other matters brought before the committee of inquiry, in the majority of eases, were taken from the Duncan report. There was no secret about the investigation that was under way at the instance of the department, and if the investigating committee had not been constituted, the process of cleaning up the department would have gone on and would have proceeded, perhaps, more rapidly. I do not say this in any way to disparage the work of the committee; but I do say that from the moment that committee began its sittings I have dismissed no employee we could possibly retain in the service or engaged no persons we could possibly get along without. I do not think there have been more than three dismissals and possibly not more than that number of appointments since the investigation started. I wanted to turn the whole thing over to the committee in order that they might direct the operations of the department as they thought best1 and carry out the authority with which they were vested by the House in the most effective way. My hon. friend the hon. member for Vancouver Centre attempted to exercise authority during that period as Minister of Customs and Excise. He went over to the department and gave his own personal instructions to the acting deputy minister, Mr. Taylor, and told him how to carry on and who to engage in connection with a certain case in the city of Regina.
That is absolutely wrong.
I am not blaming my hon. friend for that. I do not know what is wrong about it. That is what my hon. friend admitted himself in his own correspondence.
No.
My hon. friend went over to see Mr. Taylor, who is a very efficient employee, and gave him instructions.
No.
He gave him facts in confidence.
Will the minister permit me?
Yes.

I gave Mr. Taylor no instructions whatever. I handed him all the information and left the matter with him. I did not know who they were retaining; I knew nothing whatever about it. I gave him no instructions and gave him no recommendations other than this one thing: I asked that the case be prosecuted to the limit-that is all.

The letter reads:
Some weeks ago there came into my possession certain very damaging evidence of extensive excise frauds, forgeries of bogus labels, possession of customs seals, etc. on the part of certain notorious individuals an that city. I at once realized that; if these were exposed before the committee, it would probably result in the destruction of evidence that would bring about a conviction, and I realized it was more of a police case, than one for investigation before the committee.
I took the matter up with Mr. Taylor, now acting chief of tile Department of Customs and Excise. At this point I wish to state that in my estimation Mr. Taylor has been and is doing his best in the case. It appears, however, that certain influences in the government ranks are exercised to prevent this case from being successfully handled. The facts are as follows:
1. I handed all my confidential information to Mr. Taylor in confidence.
In confidence so far 33 names were concerned.

Yes.
I handed all my confidential information to Mr. Taylor in confidence.
Not much in that.

No, certainly not. My hon. friend will go to Mr. Taylor and he will say "I will allow you to tell the minister that 1 place the case in your hands, but I ask you to retain in confidence the information I gave you and not to tell the minister the names of the people against whom action is to be taken."
No, that is not it.
"In confidence so far as names are concerned?"
Confidence in so far as certain names mentioned being published and nothing else-no other reservations.
That is not what the letter says.
Oh yes.

My hon. friend's interpretation may be that, it means in confidence only so far as the publication of names is concerned; I do not know what Mr. Taylor's

Customs Inquiry-Mr. Botvin
understanding was, but I know the confidence was so well kept that the minister did not know anything about it.
It was stopped very shortly after he had learned the facts.

The minister did not know until he received a copy of thi3 letter yesterday anything whatever concerning the case. I ask my hon. friend to accept that as a true statement. Yesterday the Prime Minister was kind enough to give me a copy of the letter written to him by the hon. member for Vancouver Centre, and that was the first time I learned that the Royal Canadian Mounted Police were working upon this particular case at Regina, the first time I ever knew that any man named Bryant had represented the department, and the first time I ever knew that a man named Anderson ever conducted any case for the government in Regina.
The Minister of Justice knew about it.

That may be. The attorneys were always appointed by the Minister of Justice. Then there is the Cohen case. The letter says it has been dragging through the courts since last October, that Cohen is a rich, influential citizen of Montreal and a notorious smuggler, and that the chief of the preventive service did not know anything whatever of the frame-up. Referring to the Royal Canadian Mounted Police, my hon. friend from Vancouver, when he made his speech on the 2nd February, stated that there was no better body of men in the world.
I agree with it now. My hon. friend need not bother about that. Take it as read.
I will take the statement as read. I thank the hon. member for his confirmation.
Leave them alone and they will do their duty.

The Cohen case was confided to them for the very same reason that the hon. member for Centre Vancouver did not want to confide the Regina case to the chief preventive officer in whom he had no confidence.

No my hon. friend is
wrong.

The chief of the preventive service was at the beck and call of my hon. friend for Vancouver Centre from the beginning of the inquiry to the end, part of the time authorized by resolution, and part of [Mr. Boivin.J
the time not authorized. The chief of the preventive service placed in the hands of the hon. member for Vancouver Centre copies of certain documents that the hon. member moved for after he had the copies in his possession.
I do not recall what they are.
I could give the hon. member a list of them. They are in connection with the correspondence and the files from Bisaillon's office in Montreal.

In justice to that officer, whatever blame the minister wants to attach to me, I wish to say that he did not hand me that correspondence, and as far as I know he has never handed me any correspondence except the files of the department. The minister is exceedingly unfair to him when he says that Wilson was at my beck and call; that is entirely wrong. He never acted, as far as I know in any instance, except under orders and direction of the committee- never.

Before the applause subsides, I would like to ask the hon. member if it is not true that in connection with eight, nine or more of the cases brought before the committee, Wilson was not asked to take the files and prepare a precis and hand it to the committee, so that they would have a better case presented to them next day.

Never so far as I know, did Mr. Wilson under any circumstances, except under an open order of the committee, prepare any precis. I do not remember a single instance of that kind, and certainly Wilson would have been derelict in his duty had he not obeyed the orders of the committee.

If Mr. Wilson was such an able officer-and that is the admission I wanted to get from the lips of my hon. friend-if he was under the orders of the committtee, :f he was in close communion with my hon. friend for a period of four and a half months-
That is wrong.

-if my hon. friend has such great confidence in Mr. Wilson, why did he not confide to him, as the chief of the preventive service, the Regina case that he took over to the acting deputy minister of the department and asked him not to mention it?

I will tell my hon. friend why; the acting head of the department was

Customs Inquiry-Mr. Boivin
Mr. Taylor, the assistant deputy minister, the proper official with whom the matter ought to have 'been taken up.
I thank my hon. friend for the reason he has given. The acting head was the deputy minister.
I did not say that. The acting deputy minister-the assistant.
The hon. member went to the acting deputy minister and asked him to confide in these two special officers of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police.
No, I made no suggestion, but he suggested it, and I heartily concurred, and had the mounted police been left alone the case would have gone on merrily.
There was no request from my hon. friend that the matter be referred to the chief preventive officer.
Why should I make the suggestion?
Because you wish to make it a crime now that another case was conducted without it being referred to the same officer. In the Cohen case the matter was confided to the Royal Canadian Mounted Police.
Does the hon. minister suggest that the chief preventive officer conspired in any way with members of the committee? I ask the question in fairness to Mr. Wilson, who is a personal friend of mine.

I am very glad that Mr. Wilson has such an influential friend as the hon. member for Mount Royal, but I do say that a man who, like Mr. Wilson, has always obeyed the orders of the committee and frequently disobeyed the orders of his minister certainly does not deserve all this commendation. I will say that a man who receives and transports liquor from one province to another for other officials until he receives a certain appointment and who ceases doing it after that appointment has been given to him, is not one of those officers who deserve the highest commendation and praise even from my hon. friend.
The minister forgets that Mr. Wilson was chief preventive officer long before the question of the transportation of liquor came up.
The minister is absolutely wrong.

My hon. friend says that I
am absolutely wrong. I may be unduly severe, but I am not absolutely wrong?

Will the minister allow
me to interject?
Some hon. MEMBERS. Sit down.

My hon. friend spoke for
over two hours and a half.
Only an hour and a half.

I think he should at least
let me reply.

He is absolutely unfair
to a man who cannot defend himself.

I want to point out that
in the Cohen matter certain information that had been brought to our attention was confided to the Royal Canadian Mounted Police because the preventive officers had informed me some time previously that while Mr. Cohen had been arrested by Mr. Knox, they were not in a position to find any of the other conspirators in the smuggling of the goods. One of these men who is now under arrest and before the courts in Montreal had made the statement that he had influence with not Mr. Wilson-I do not want to accuse Mr. Wilson of anything of that nature-but with Mr. Knox. That statement was reported to me. It may have been a misleading statement; it may not have been true; but it was for that reason that instead of confiding the case to Mr. Wilson or Mr. Knox, I instructed that it be given to the Royal Canadian Mounted Police. If I have been unjust to Mr. Wilson-
'Grossly unjust.

-I may have been somewhat severe in some of my strictures on him, but I will say this, that in many cases to my personal knowledge confidences given to Mr. Wilson have not been respected. Information was given by Mr. Wilson to members of the committee before it was given to the minister himself during the conduct of the committee. That is an absolutely fair and true statement. I regret having interjected the Other matter in reply to the hon. member for Mount Royal.

If that be
so, I withdraw my remarks.

I do not pretend to deserve special consideration in the administration of the department, but will my hon. friends allow me to say at least what I have done since I took possession of the office? The very first act was to start this investigation in the city
Customs Inquiry-Mr. Boivin

of Montreal The moment Inspector Duncan made his first report I had no hesitation in asking council to dismiss Mr. Bisaillon, in suspending some of the employees who were near to him in that office and in removing from the preventive service to the port many of the officers who had given faithful service for many years to the preventive service but who had been closely associated with Mr. Bisaillon. They have remained there ever since. Many of them have been found absolutely blameless by the committee. I hope they will return to their former positions in the immediate future.
As regards the regulations concerning automobiles not only am I prepared to follow out the recommendations contained in the report, but we started months ago putting similar regulations into effect. The instructions now given in the Department of Customs are that every time it is possible for a United States automobile to be returned to that country that procedure shall be followed, and the penalty imposed on Americans who come into Canada without reporting at the border shall be made as low as possible in order that all United States cars may be returned and not placed as a glut on the Canadian market in competition with our Canadian cars.
We have given instructions to do away with the practice, which was becoming prevalent in the department, of customs officers using smuggled and seized cars which had been confiscated and placed at their disposal, of their riding around in cars that had been seized but not confiscated or not sold. In two or three instances the cars were later claimed by the United States owner and they were returned. Instructions have been given to our officers now never to take over or use a seized car except where it is necessary to bring it from the point of seizure to the garage. Every car that cannot be returned to the United States must be sold and officers in the department entitled to cars will be supplied with Canadian oars for their use.
We have endeavoured to get new boats to place on the coast of the Maritime Provinces to prevent smuggling there, but unfortunately matters have been delayed by the fact that our supply has not yet been voted. Hon. members preferred to have us wait until the committee made its- report before voting us the supply required for the preventive service and I did not desire to increase the service until the supply is voted.
There are in the report many recommendations which we shall be in a position to carry out this year. There are some recommenda-

tions which I fear it will be impossible to embody in legislation until the next session of parliament. But I can assure my hon. friend once again, speaking for myself as minister of the department, that the regulations required will be made at the earliest possible opportunity and that every honest effort will be made to carry out the recommendations of the report, as it is finally adopted and approved by this House of Commons.
At six o'clock the House took recess.
After Recess
The House resumed at eight o'clock.

subtopic: RED LAKE AND NORTHWESTERN RAILWAY COMPANY

speechtext:
The House resumed, from June 18, consideration in committee of Bill No. 95, to incorporate the Red Lake and Northwestern Railway Company-Mr. Heenan-Mr. Duff in the chair.
On section 1

Incorporation.

subtopic: RED LAKE AND NORTHWESTERN RAILWAY COMPANY
speechtext:
When this bill was before the House on Friday last objection was taken that it had not been reprinted as amended and, further, that we had no statement from the Minister of Railways (Mr. Dunning) as to the policy of the government with regard to the granting of charters for railways such as the one here contemplated. This is an independent company asking for a charter and, as I pointed out the other evening, as a result

Red Lake Railway Company
of the indiscriminate granting of railway charters in Canada, without regard to public convenience and the absence of any well defined system controlling rivalry, we find ourselves in Canada with two competitive lines of railway, the government having been forced to assume responsibility for upwards of 22,000 miles. There can be no question that the Canadian people have paid dearly for their railway experience, and it passes my understanding how the government can sit quietly by and allow such a bill as this to come up repeatedly without offering some explanation of its policy in regard to the issuing of charters. This particular bill has been under consideration in different forms during the present session; yet the Minister of Railways sits here without volunteering any information to assist the House in coming to a conclusion in the matter. The Minister of Finance (Mr. Robb) himself on Friday last agreed that we were entitled to some definite statement regarding the policy of the Department of Railways on the granting of charters.
We have seen for years now private companies applying for charters with no intention whatever of building any railways, and always coming back for an extension of time, so that in the long run many of these charters have had to be cancelled entirely. In other 'cases roads have been constructed without regard to convenience or economy, with the result that the country has suffered. In the present, instance we do not know -whether the proposed railway will be built, the only information we have being that a blanket charter is asked for to enable a company to construct a line from somewhere near Hud-san bay down to the Canadian National system. The House ought to know just what the company will do, and whether it sincerely intends to build the road. I do not believe the people mentioned in this charter have any intention of going on with this road themselves. They may represent someone else, but it is quite evident that if this road is operated successfully it will have to be operated by the Canadian National Railway System, and if that is the case by all means let the Canadian National Railway System ask for a charter and go on with the construction of this road, and see that the road is built where it should go and not where it will suit the convenience of some promoters -who may possibly intend to dispose of their charter after having secured it.
I know it will be argued that there is provision in this bill that unless the company does a certain amount of work during the coming year the charter will lapse. That
provision has been in bills before, and we have seen the companies coming back time after time, after having spent a little money, and have their charters renewed. This renewal of charters has been a common practice for years, and I think we should have a clear and definite statement from the minister as to what the government propose doing. We recently had the experience of this government. granting a charter for the construction of a road adjacent to the Transcontinental and Temiskaming and Northern Ontario railways; bonds were guaranteed to the extent of $5,000,000, while an injunction was taken out against the province of Ontario, who did not ask for a dollar, in order to prevent them from building a road there. The people interested were more anxious for a connection with the mining centres tributary to the Temiskaming and Northern Ontario railway than for a road from O'Brien into that territory. I do think the minister should make a clear and definite statement as to what the government intend doing in this connection so that, parliament may have a proper idea of what the passing of this bill may mean.

subtopic: RED LAKE AND NORTHWESTERN RAILWAY COMPANY
speechtext:
I regret not having had
an opportunity to discuss this matter on a former occasion. I think at one time the bill was talked out, and although many of the members speaking on that occasion asked for a statement from the minister he was not given an opportunity to make one, the time passes so quickly. On another occasion I regret to say that I was not in the House.
The position to-day is the same as it has been for many years. Those who desire to incorporate railway companies in Canada come before parliament with a private bill; that bill is referred to the Railway committee and there examined. The contents of such bills are communicated to the Minister of Railways, who examines them from the point of view of their relationship to other railways now existing or projected. In this case I had the bill examined from the point of view of its relationship to or effect on the Canadian National Railway system, and I was assured that the Canadian National did not propose itself to build into the territory affected at. present. That territory is not regarded by the management as being proven from a branch line traffic point of view, and they therefore do not intend to ask the Minister of Railways to request the necessary money from parliament for the construction of a Canadian National branch. That being the case, the Department of Railways made no
Red Lake Railway Company

objection before the committee to the granting of a private charter.
But I would like the committee to remember that the right to grant charters of this kind is inherent in parliament itself. It is true that we might have a government policy of refusal of all private charters. If we had complete government ownership of railways from one end of Canada to the other; if we had no private ownership of railways at all, then manifestly the policy of the government would be to ask parliament to refuse to grant charters for new lines. Inasmuch, however, as we have in Canada at present both government owned railways and privately owned railways, the position is as it always has been, that parliament itself on the advice of the railway committee, which presumably examines the merits of each case, decides whether or not additional private charters shall be granted. In this case I am informed that the line opens up entirely new territory, connecting at one end with the Canadian National main line and at the other with the Hudson Bay railway. Let me repeat that the management of the Canadian National Railways are not prepared at present to recommend to parliament the expenditure of public money necessaiy to build a branch line into this area. That being the case the Canadian National Railway leaves the matter entirely in the hands of the Railway committee of this House to determine whether, in all the circumstances, private parties should be permitted so to do.

speechtext:
I have not given
particular attention to this measure, and I am free to admit that there may be some special considerations appertaining to it, but on the general subject of policy with respect *to private charters I am far from satisfied1 with the statement .made by the Minister of Railways (Mr. Dunning). He says that we have a government owned system which is not itself a monopoly; we have as well a great privately owned system and consequently, under these circumstances, the government simply examines any application from the point of view of the desirability of reserving the territory to the National system. If the government come to the conclusion that the territory is not such as the National system now desires to enter they simply leave it to the Railway committee of parliament to decide whether or not a private company shall get a charter.
I would like to suggest to the minister that the time has passed when any administration in this country should content itself with such

an attitude. It is true that we have not a government monopoly; it is equally true that we have no competitive system with a variety of railway companies such as other countries enjoy, the United States for example. We have proceeded in the evolution of our railway policy far beyond the point reached) in most other countries, and having reached the stage where we have one great publicly owned system and another great privately owned system we certainly have reached the point where we must consider whether we will grant any more charters to heterogeneous companies here, there and everywhere, for the construction of little one hundred or two hundred mile railways. These railways, when they are constructed, are certain either to be failures, thus bringing discredit upon Canadian finance, or if they are successful they are bound on the one hand to detract from the earning capacity of the great private system and thereby hold up railway rates, or to detract from the earning capacity of the great publicly owned system and therefore injure the country as a whole. One of these two results must ensue from the creation of privately owned railway companies anywhere, in competition with the two great systems we already have. I cannot see how any result beneficial to the people generally can ensue which could not have been attained much better by another route. Let me .repeat:	If
the railway proves a failure as a commercial venture then there is the repercussion back on Canadian credit, which is injurious to the country as a whole. If it proves a success it simply means that the new railway has invaded territory which in the general interest should have been conceded either to the private company on the one hand or reserved for the public company on the other. I do not think this reasoning can be very well challenged.
If these are the only consequences, all of them are injurious to the country, and for my part it would take a very powerful array of special circumstances to convince me that there should be an exception made in respect of a road either to Red lake or to any other territory. I would think the government Should very carefully consider whether or not we have reached the time when the granting of private railway charters to third companies, new organizations, should be done away with once and for all.

speechtext:
There is a great deal of force in what my right hon. friend says in thus connection. He recognizes, of course, that the adoption of tba* attitude absolutely would

be an entirely new departure, and one which therefore should be given very careful consideration. May I also point out for his consideration-and in this connection I am not discussing the merits of the present bill or of the proposed railway-that the provinces also have the power to grant railway charters; they can and do, and in the last sessions of many of the provincial legislatures charters have been granted to private parties for the construction of railroads entirely, of course, within the borders of the province. So the object sought by my right hon. friend cannot be wholly attained merely by this parliament refusing the granting of such charters. Also I am informed'-I should say this in fairness to the present proposal-that the proposed line will in any event be a feeder to the Canadian National system and will connect only with Canadian National lines.
We are in this awkward position in considering the matter. Parliament from time to time gives consideration to branch lines proposals put forward by the Canadian National and by the Canadian Pacific railway. It may! very well be that for reasons which seem good to the government or to parliament for the time being, it is not advisable to extend into an area such as the one now under discussion, and the important and difficult question which prevents me agreeing altogether with my right hon. friend is this:	Shall we
say, because parliament cannot see its way clear to vote public moneys for the construction of a line that therefore that particular area of country shall be left without railway transportation? That is a difficult question, and it is rendered still more difficult in its relation to general policy by the other fact which I mentioned, that every provincial legislature in Canada has the power to grant railway charters within its own borders.
In connection with the present case, inquiry was made of the government of the province of Ontario, and I understand that the premier of that province indicated that the government of Ontario had no objection to the granting of this charter.
