dition by the frequent granting of charters to private companies. It is something we must stop.
There is no hurry for this road. As a matter of fact Red lake is being supplied to-day by communication from the air, and a good service is being provided, with people and supplies getting in and out of that area with little trouble. If there is anything in this Red lake proposition it will show itself during this summer; then the Canadian National Railway may be prepared to build into that territory and Manitoba would be in a position to decide whether or not it would do so. There is no hurry for this proposition at all, except on the part of certain gentlemen who want to follow the example that was set in this House by the government a very short time ago in connection with the building of a line into the Rouyn gold field in the province of Quebec. The Canadian National is serv< ing the Rouyn territory, and the province of Ontario, by its enterprise, has covered the whole gold and silver fields of Ontario with the Temiskaming and Northern Ontario railway, which has a dozen branches through all that territory.

I know, but the mining country of northern Ontario is being absolutely served now by public owned railroads, either the Canadian National which goes through Sudbury and all that mining district, or the Temiskaming and Northern Ontario railway, which goes through Cobalt, Kirkland lake, up to Timmins, and through all the great gold fields in the province. We are only beginning to develop the mining camps in Ontario; they are growing every day. Gowganda is coming back, and all we want to do is to keep that country for the two publicly owned lines. I believe these two lines will eventually co-operate in some way to cover the whole of that country. If we have made a success of the Canadian National covering the whole continent, cannot we do

better by building our own railway into this territory, into the mining fields of Ontario and Quebec, of Manitoba and the whole west? We are supplying these fields to-day either by the National lines or the provincially owned lines of Ontario, and the people are getting extensions just as fast as they are warranted. I am convinced the Temiskaming and Northern Ontario will build this summer from a terminal called Elk Lake into the Gowganda mining camp, on to Leonard and Shining Tree, and from there to Westree, where they will connect up with the Transcontinental. We do not want any more of these private companies. We have had enough of them. We have had to take up the mess they left, and pay for it. We have got far more miles of railway than we want in this country, simply because we have been over-railroaded and over-exploited by private individuals who came to. parliament and got- charters. So I intend to move, Mr. Chairman, that this bill be sent back to the committee and in that way taken off the order paper. We shall then see w'hat the developments will be in the Red Lake district. If it is shown that there is necessity for this railway it will be built; I have no doubt the Canadian National will build it if the occasion arises. In the meantime the aeroplane service will supply the necessities of that camp in every way. It is already giving a mail and express service, and taking in passengers. They can go in very quickly by aeroplane, whereas t'he journey now takes from two to three days by railway and waterways. I am also told that the Ontario government now have before them plans for the building of a roadway from Hudson right into Red lake. In the meantime let us stop this over-exploitation of railway charters by private individuals. such a letter if the Ontario government had any such intention as my hon. friend stated. One would think from the discussion which has taken place this evening that private investors ought to be debarred from developing this district. I notice, however, that only applies where the district is unorganized and without boards of trade or councils that could make representations to this House. For instance, in the Railway committee this morning we had under consideration a private undertaking for the tunnelling of the Detroit river. No one in that committee ever suggested that such a tunnel would take away traffic from the Canadian National Railways, and yet as a matter of fact it would. However, no objection was raised to it. Then, too, there seems to be no objection as to private concerns operating in Winnipeg, Toronto or Montreal; but when it comes to :a remote district, Where the population is scarce, and where the proposition is one that everybody can block and make a political football of, private investors seem to be .debarred. What we want is a railway in the Red lake district, and we care not whether it is built by the Canadian National, the *Canadian Pacific, or a private corporation. The Canadian National Railways have already announced, through the minister or his deputy, that they have no intention of building immediately into that country.
Now what is the worst that can happen if this bill carries? A private corporation can invest their own money in the building of a railroad that will be a feeder to the Canadian National railway if it is a success. If the enterprise is not a success, it is the investors that will !be out; they will have lost their money. I have received twenty-one telegrams from clubs, municipalities, and development boards in the northern part of the country asking that this railway charter be granted, and I hope the House will see to it that that part of the country is not held back from development. So far as the Ontario government is concerned, they granted a charter the session before last to a private concern for a railway right north of the twin aities of Port Arthur and Fort William. Evidently therefore the Ontario .government are not blocking avenues to
private investors. The hon. member for North Winnipeg (Mr. Heaps) stated that the Manitoba government have granted a charter to some private concern to build into the Red lake district, and are backing the enterprise to the extent of $25,000 a mile. Let me point out to my hon. friend that it is impossible for the Manitoba government to do that; they cannot grant a charter for a railway to build into Ontario, they can only charter a railway to the Manitoba boundary. What we need in that part of the country is transportation for carrying supplies and people into the Red lake territory, to which hundreds of people are flocking daily. The hon. member for South York (Mr. Maclean) advises people to go in by aeroplane. Well, the aeroplane may be a quick method of transportation, but there are a lot of people who prefer travelling by railway to travelling in the air. On behalf of the people in that part of the country I appeal to the House to grant this charter.

To me there seems
to be some little misunderstanding with regard to the application that is before the House in reference to this Red lake charter. In the first place such a branch line cannot be a competitor of the Canadian National railways. Whatever else it may become, it cannot compete with that system. The only line to which it can deliver any traffic it may gather is the Canadian National Railways. It is running at right angles hundreds of miles away from any other branch line whatsoever. When this bill was first before the committee I asked that it be held up until we got further information with respect to those who were promoting it, and the reasons why the charter was being asked for. Having inquired into the matter I came to the conclusion that parliament could safeguard itself and still allow this charter to be granted, it being clearly understood that people putting any money into the enterprise are doing

Red Lake Railway Company
so with their eyes wide open and will lose that money if the line is unsuccessful. My understanding, after making inquiries, is that in the first instance the people who are going in there in an effort to develop the country are desirous of building a light railway or tramway in order to get in the machinery and equipment necessary for development purposes. If the country proves to be what those who are interested hope and believe it will, the promoters, having built a light railway or tramway, would have a vested right . and could go ahead and build a line that would serve as a feeder to the Canadian National railways. Or the road itself might be taken over by the Canadian National Railways if they so desired; but that system would be under no obligation whatever to take the line off the hands of the promoters. If this charter is refused it simply means, unless the Canadian National Railways are prepared to go ahead and build the line, that the men who are in that district endeavouring to develop the country have no means by which they can get their equipment in. It is all very well to talk about bringing in supplies by aeroplane. Some people and mail matter can go in by aeroplane; but you cannot take diamond drilling outfits and hoisting machinery, with all the things that go to equip a mine, by areoplane. There is provision in connection with this charter by which the line can ultimately be extended, but they must do everything they are going to do this year, as I understand it. If the country did so develop that they could go right straight across from the line of the Canadian National to the Hudson bay, they would then be serving the Canadian National as feeders at both points. To my mind the statement that
rMr. Nicholson.]

Mr. _ EVANS: On former occasions I have opposed this project for well defined reasons, and I have had no cause to change my mind. speechtext:
I stated that I had received twenty-one telegrams from the people of that country.

Red Lake Railway Company

subtopic: RED LAKE AND NORTHWESTERN RAILWAY COMPANY
speechtext:
The hon. gentleman, if he wishes, can speak again when I am through. These people ask for a charter. As soon as they obtain it they will have something for sale, and for sale it will be sooner or later, when either the Canadian National or the Canadian Pacific will have to take it over. When the need for a railway is made known in that district I shall be one of the first to advocate its construction by the Canadian National Railway. This country is commited to government ownership, and since we have over fifty per cent of our railways under government ownership and operation, the reasonable thing to do is to go forward and develop a complete system of government ownership and operation of our railway services. These roads must be operated and controlled by the people in the interest of all the people. It is a public utility and therefore should never pass out of the hands of the people. If we grant a charter in this case it will be a precedent for granting further charters for like branches, and in the future we shall have a railway problem even greater than that which is on our hands at the present time. Why should Canada take a step backward and create a precedent in this instance? Out of sixty-five countries of the world, fifty-one own and operate their railways. It is interesting to note that of all the countries Belgium is the only one that has owned and operated her railways from the beginning. It has often been said that government ownership is not a success when applied to public utilities, but I do not think there is even one advocate of private ownership who will say that our postal sendee should go back into private hands. The greatest argument for government ownership of railways is the fact that out of all the countries of the world fifty nations have, found private ownership a failure. I am giving the House this information on the authority of one Mr. E. B. Biggar, who wrote some articles on this subject some years ago. All the great dominions, apart from Canada and India, operate their railways through government ownership and control. In addition to that, out of seventeen crown colonies and protectorates in the British Empire, twelve have government ownership of railways. Surely therefore the reasonable thing for Canada to do is to go forward with government-owned and operated systems of railways. These countries and colonies are among the most highly developed and civilized in the whole world. They have adopted government ownership, and not through lack of private enterprise either. I think it can very well be said, particularly since the war, that the people of all countries are coming to
realize that public utilities should be owned and operated by the people in the interests of the whole people, and not as a source of private gain for private companies. Indeed it would be just as reasonable, in my view, to have our highway system owned and operated by private concerns as to place our railways in private hands with the one idea only of private gain. Shall Canada now take a step backward and grant a charter to a company which has no other idea than to exploit the public and our natural resources for private gain? Surely we have done with that policy regarding our railways. Since we have more ithan fifty per cent of our railways under government ownership and control, I say again it is the reasonable thing to go forward towards a complete system. It does not take much imagination to see the immense unearned increment that will in the future, through growth of population and industrial development, accrue to our private railway companies. All this must be appropriated from now on for the use of the state and not given away for the enrichment of a particular class in the community or a particular company which has no other idea than to exploit the people for its own private gain.
The whole sum of life is no doubt composed of trifles, and it is of such trifles as this charter represents that the great sum of over $2,000,000,000 is made up which represents our railway debt. This little charter, according to one of the promoters, represents just the beginning of another transcontinental railway. It is only part of a scheme to tap the tremendous resources of our hinterland and to exploit the people by so doing, to exploit the public in railway service and deplete our natural resources for private gain. Mr. Biggar, to whom I have already referred, has laid down a few well-defined rules regarding the public utilities of a country. Of the railways he has this to say:
X. The railways of a country are its main highways and therefore should not pass out of the control of the people.
2.	There is no source of revenue for a railway other than the rates imposed for carrying persons and goods.
3.	This revenue is raised, not from any hidden fountain of wealth within the railway itself, buit from the proceeds derived from the economic activities of the entire people.
4.	By the division of labour in the modem state everyone who earns and spends money contributes to the cost of railway service, and this cost enters into practically every article used by the people.
5.	The maintenance of a nation's means of communication is a function of sovereignty, which should not be permitted to be exercised by private individuals for their own benefit.
6.	Since ail the people contribute to the cost of railway service, railway rates become essentially a national tax. And in all highly developed countries,

Red Lake Railway Company
railway rates make up the largest element in taxation. It is of fundamental importance that the people should retain control of the machinery through which they are subject to taxation.
The people of Canada have only the satisfaction by taxing themselves of making good the yearly deficit on the railways that we have at present. It seems unreasonable to add to our burden by projects of this kind. The granting of this charter will mark the beginning of a system calculated to cripple the National system. Efforts have already been made to create in the minds of the public an attitude that will prepare the way for complete private control of our railway service. The privately-owned system is often pointed to as such a wonderful success in comparison with the nationally-owned system, which certainly from the very beginning consisted of just so many mistakes from a utility standpoint. We are -all supposed to jubilate when this great -private company makes known its annual [DOT]earnings and dividends and the great surplus earnings that are yearly carried over to its reserve. Mr. Speaker, when the House rose at six o'clock I had almost concluded my remarks. It was at that time my intention to reply to the allegation contained in the amendment to this *effect:
The Prime Minister and the government had knowledge for some considerable time of the rapid degenera-

t.ion of the Department of Customs and Excise, and their failure to take prompt and effective remedial action is wholly indefensible.
I intended to reply ,to that, but I will not take the time to cite the correspondence exchanged between Mr. Sparks, president of the Commercial Protective Association, and the Prime Minister. It is all of record; it speaks for itself. It will diow that from the very moment that the Commercial Protective Association was organized, they received the most hearty co-operation from the different members of the government with whom they communicated. It will show that both from the Prime Minister and from the Minister of Finance (Mr. Robb) they received the utmost aid and assistance. The preventive officers that they chose themselves as being the best available men to prevent the nefarious offence of smuggling were engaged and paid by t'he government. They were later placed upon the staff of the preventive service, but still left at the disposal of the Commercial Protective Association. These officers, while they were paid by the government, remained practically in the employ of the association until late in the autumn of 1925, when the political situation changed matters considerably and when one of the officers of the Commercial Protective Association deemed it advisable-and I have no complaint as to that -to stump the country on the same platform with the leader of the opposition (Mr. Meighen). He devoted his talents and his energies to the interests of the Conservative party and did his utmost to defeat the government now in power; and not only did he exert his efforts during the campaign, but as results will show he pursued them more or less successfully thereafter, from the very moment the votes had been counted until the present occasion. As I observed this afternoon, however, I desire to pay tribute to Mr. Sparks to the extent that the report which was submitted to t'he committee in printed pamphlet form by himself on behalf of his associates is well worthy of note is free from political considerations and will receive careful1 consideration at the hands of the government.
The Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) will be shown in this correspondence, and especially in the evidence of Mr. Sparks before the committee, as having done all he possibly could to meet the situation at that time, and I wish to assure the House emphatically that there is no reason for hon. gentlemen opposite to attempt to place responsibility for the conduct of the Department of Customs and Excise upon the Prime Minister or any other member of the government since

Customs Inquiry-Mr. Boimn
my entry into the cabinet. Neither the Prime Minister nor any of my colleagues have at any time attempted to interfere with the discharge of my duties. For that reason, if the words "political associates" embodied in the amendment are intended to include my right hon. leader and my colleagues in the proposed motion of censure, I wish to dissociate them from the amendment and bear alone the censure it implies.
I wish to make one observation for the benefit of hon. gentlemen opposite who shortly will be called upon to support this amendment :
Your committee deplores the practice, as revealed by the evidence, of certain men influential in public life to direct appeals to the minister to relax and depart from the proper administration of his department for reasons of political expediency.
Your committee is of the opinion that this practice is detrimental to the best interests of the country and prejudicial to the administration of the department.
I trust that hon. gentlemen opposite w'll bear in mind this fact, that since the commencement of this session members of parliament have come to me with the request to intercede in behalf of some of their electors in cases which in some respects were similar to that of Moses Aziz. Only the other day certain hon. gentlemen were in my office asking that I refrain from imposing a fine on a dealer who unfortunately had exposed his tobacco on his shelves without having revenue stamps affixed to the box; while others have approached me in the interest of civil servants who have been short in their accounts but who have subsequently made amends. I hope that those hon. gentlemen on the opposite side, before voting on the proposed amendment, will reflect for a moment, that the life of the Minister of Customs is perhaps, to use a popular expression, not all that it is cracked up to be. I do not pretend to be at the head of one c,f the most important departments of government; far from it. I do however claim to be at the head of the department whch is probably the most difficult to administer. I would remind hon. gentlemen opposite that when men are obeying the customs and excise laws of the country they never appeal to the Minister of Customs; there is no necessity for so doing. They deal directly with the officials of the department and their way is made easy. But the moment any member finds that an elector has transgressed the law, though sometimes unwittingly, sometimes unwillingly, the tendency inevitably is to come to the minister with a request for clemency. Occasionally the offender is a doctor who is called across the line in his automobile to attend a patient and who is obliged to cross 14011-308
at a point where there is no customs office, so that he is unable to report. Or, it may be, he finds it imperative to cross the line after nightfall. -Sometimes it is an American citizen who does not know that he has crossed the boundary and is therefore on Canadian territory without having reported his car. There are various cases of a technical nature in which a judge, applying the strict letter of the law, would in all probability impose the entire penalty; and such cases are submitted to the minister by members of parliament day after day. One case was laid before me the day before yesterday in which possibly it might be a hardship to exact the fine. A young girl who had recently been employed in a certain store, while the person in charge was absent through illness, failed to open a box of tobacco in the proper manner and so exposed the article on the shelves without having put the excise stamps upon it. If I had granted the request which was made in that case, and had refrained from imposing the fine, I would have been accused, in the event of the matter hav ng been brought before the committee, and if the member of parliament applying to me for consideration had been a Liberal member, of having acted with a view to obtaining political party advantage.
I hope, Mr. Speaker, that I shall be believed by hon. members on both sides of the House when I declare that, if it is my privilege to remain in charge of the department, members not only of the Conservative party but of -the liberal party as well, and my Progressive friends and the Independent members of this House will all be treated alike and that whatever discretion may be left to me will be exercised on the merits of the ease. I do say, however, that if this House of Commons were to remove that discretion it would be rendering the greatest service possible to the Minister of Customs. If it were possible for the minister to direct the general policy of the department, without any power to exercise discretion in any instance, the charge in the Moses Aziz case, which will be launched against me in a few moments by my hon. friend from Hamilton (Mr. Bell), would not be before the House to-night. But I submit that if discretion is to be left to the minister, then the circumstances surrounding any case must be taken into consideration. If it is felt that he should not exercise any discretion at all, then let that discretion be removed. But when that discretion is removed, do not hold him responsible for 'his inability to settle cases nor convey to the people of Canada the impres-

1856	COMMONS
Customs Inquiry-Mr. Bell (Hamilton)
sion that cabinet ministers in Ottawa are allpowerful and that they are clothed with the functions of a judge.
I do not want to detain the House a moment longer, but again I wish to dissociate my colleagues from the motion of censure contained in the amendment moved by my hon. friend from Vancouver Centre. As 1 tried to explain this afternoon that since the moment I became a member of the government I have renounced my private affairs and abandoned my family life. I have devoted sixteen hours every day, and an occasional Sunday, to the service of this country; and if as a reward I am to be voted out of office ito-night, either alone or with my colleagues, I am willing to attribute the action of parliament to the payment of the debt of service that I owe the country I love most, our own country, Canada.

subsubtopic: RETORT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE-MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE AND AMENDMENT THERETO.
speechtext:
I do not know when there has come to me as a member of, shall I say, the late Customs committee, a moment filled with quite so much gratification as that which I experienced this afternoon when my hon. friend from Vancouver Centre (Mr. Stevens) rose to his feet and was greeted as he was by this House. I could conceive of nothing more fitting, more reasonable and more just than that he who has shown such great courage, such great loyalty and such gTeat devotion to the affairs of this country and to all whose responsibility he has undertaken to see through, should render to the House an account of his stewardship. I am glad to be able to add to the remarks that he has made, as well as to those of the hon. gentleman who has just taken his seat (Mr. Boivin), the expression of our appreciation of the loyal, kindly, splendid service that has been rendered in this inquiry by the chairman of the committee. I can only say of the chairman, not having had the privilege of his acquaintance until coming here this term, that I feel the experience gained in my association with him has been such as to command a lasting friendship which, for my part, I shall be very proud to hold.
And, Sir, there is one other of those who laboured in connection with the work of this committee who, I think in simple, common justice, should be mentioned to this House tonight; I refer to Mr. R. L. Calder, K.C., who acted as committee counsel. The Conservative members of this committee were severely criticized in certain quarters when they readily agreed * to the selection of Mr. Calder as counsel for the committee, because it was felt that he who had been the political opponent of the present member for Mount TMr. Boivin.]
Royal (Mr. White) in the last election would perhaps have such a coloured viewpoint in the inquiry to be conducted that there would be a large measure of partisanship in his work. It is justice and not generosity to Mr. Calder to say that the element of partisanship was, from beginning to end, totally lacking. Therefore I deem it all the more unfortunate that this afternoon the Minister of Customs should have said that there was an effort made extending over some four months to attack and blacken the Department of Customs. If such an effort was made, with that loyal counsel exercising his functions and performing his duties in the most impartial way, I should like to know from what source it came. Unhappily the evidence adduced before the committee leads to but one conclusion, that the department has been blackened by those in charge, and not by this party.
The minister spoke truly when he told the House this afternoon that I, to whom has been delegated the task of saying something to the House dealing with the minister's conduct in connection with the Aziz case, would engage in that task most reluctantly; he has never spoken a truer word. It is with the greatest reluctance that I begin my task now, and I will go further and say that it is with a feeling of deep regret that I lay before the House certain facts and circumstances, unhappily both many and important, which go to show that the minister, however ready he may be to assume responsibility for the delinquencies of his party, is not one whit behind the leading members of the cabinet, including the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) himself.
As one might well believe, Mr. Speaker, I listened with the greatest of interest to the defence made by the minister this afternoon of his colleagues and of his own conduct in office, and I am bound to say that, with my familiarity with these facts of which he was speaking, if I had any doubt before of the delinquencies which had occurred, the minister's own defence resolved those doubts for me. That is why I feel that we on this side of the House approach and deal with the facts as they stand by themselves without any spirit of partisanship or prejudice. Unhappily these facts, considered even in the most favourable light, are such as to render it impossible lor any self-respecting government and any self-respecting minister to remain longer in office.
The minister is surely master of his own method of procedure in this case, and he found it necessary to begin his argument by reading a letter which he had received from a man who was named as having been de-

Customs Inquiry-Mr. Bell (Hamilton)
linquent in his duty. This man was unanimously so named by the committee, because the evidence permitted of no other conclusion. If I am wrong in saying that the minister had the opportunity, if he so desired, of placing that man's position more favourably before the committee than it actually was placed, I know the minister will correct me. The minister approached the matter in such a way as to indicate some sympathy on his part for this man who, according to the unanimous decision of the committee, had utterly failed in his duty.
The minister has told us that during his term of office he at least had the advantage of enjoying the confidence of the Prime Minister of Canada. Let me say, Sir, that it is fair comment after listening to the evidence given before the committee that some do not apparently find it very difficult to enjoy that confidence.
The report brought in by the committee, as the House already knows, dealt with a number of ways in which the department has been degenerating for the past three or four years, and made a formal finding to the effect that the degeneration, through the lack of appreciation of responsibility on the part of the preceding minister, Mr. Bureau, had been greatlj'' accelerated. Perhaps it is worthy of comment here that the majority of those who sat on that committee, although this degeneration had been continuing for some time and had recently been accelerated to a very large degree, refused to find that this degeneration- had continued under the regime of the present minister. If there was any effort made before the committee to show that in the regime of the present minister anything was done to bring the department back to its former high estate, I would be glad to have that evidence pointed out to me. I think the facts point undoubtedly to the conclusion that so far from in any way rehabilitating the department, under the present minister it has sunk to a depth never touched before.
A considerable issue has been raised in this House as to whether or not the Minister of Customs, as he wishes to put it himself, stood alone in any delinquencies with which he has been connected. I want to say that the facts show irresistibly-as I propose to demonstrate to the House by reference to these facts-that long before the present minister took up the reins of office the degeneration of that department and of the whole cabinet had set in. When the Minister of Customs took office he simply fitted into a place already prepared for him by those whose one creed had been to protect and H011-3081
encourage smugglers as against the interests of honest people.
The first official reference in the evidence given before the committee came when Mr. Sparks, who has been already referred to for his earnest work in endeavouring to remedy these bad conditions, sought an opportunity of laying before the Prime Minister the facts connected with the smuggling operations which were being conducted to the great detriment and loss of honest Canadian merchants. Referring to the first positive statement that occurs in the evidence taken before the committee, may I point out that on June 23, 1924, Sparks, not acting alone but as representing a very large number of associations of merchants, manufacturers and importers who were being robbed and plundered by the'conditions that existed through the smuggling that was then rampant in Canada, sought an opportunity of getting the assistance of the government in some effort, that might be made to put down that smuggling. On June 23, 1924, Sparks wrote to the Prime Minister, on behalf of the Businessmen's Association asking for a meeting and point,mg out that smuggling had reached such appalling proportions in the Dominion of Canada that in the Rock Island district alone the sum of over $10,000,000 was annually being lost in revenue to the Canadian people. On the 6th of August they got their meeting, and according to the evidence that was given before the committee there were present at that meeting, representing the government: the Right Hon. Mr. Mackenzie King, Hon. Jacques Bureau, Hon. Mr. Lapointe. Hon. Mr. Macdonald, Hon. Mr. Graham and Hon. J. H. King, Minister of Public Works. On the side of those who came to protest against these conditions that had grown so intolerable, were the representatives of thirteen associations of businessmen in this country, and a large number of men who did not represent any particular association but who had decided that their only course was to come before the government and beg for assistance in order that the conditions might be remedied and, if possible, that their livelihood might be saved. They saw those members of the cabinet, and on that very day they asked for a parliamentary committee to investigate those conditions and to endeavour to find a remedy. What did they get? They got nothing at all except the indifference of the government, because this government from that day on, as is shown by the record, never exerted itself on behalf of anybody but the thieves and smugglers who were pestering the businessmen of Canada. But these
4858	COMMONS
Customs Inquiry-Mr. Bell (Hamilton)
businessmen persisted in their entreaties and in their efforts, and finally, on the 1st of October, Walter Duncan was loaned to them to investigate conditions particularly in the Rock Island district, and to assist them in putting down this smuggling.
It is said that Walter Duncan was told by the Prime Minister: Pursue the smugglers closely; do not allow them to continue their operations if you can help it; put them in gaol. Duncan went out, and he ran down some of the notorious silk smugglers, a number of people operating in and out of Montreal. Then what happened? As soon as he began, as a result of his investigations, to lay facts before this government which would justify, nay, which would demand, that prosecutions should take place, the friends of the smugglers came up to Ottawa, as they had been doing consistently from time to time, and saw the ministers of the crown, and they called off every prosecution that was suggested as a result of Duncan's investigation. But these manufacturers and businessmen had no other remedy. They had been defrauded and plundered; they had no other source than ihe government to which to turn for relief, so again on December 12, 1924, Sparks wrote to the Hon. Jacques Bureau, again stressing conditions at Rock Island. The hon. member for Vancouver Centre (Mr. Stevens) referred to that letter this afternoon, but I wish briefly to direct the attention of the House to it. At page 120 of the evidence appears the letter that was written by R. P. Sparks to the Hon. Jacques Bureau, dated December 12, 1924, in which Mr. Sparks, on behalf of all these associations of businessmen whom he represented, said this:
Another matter to which reference was made was the situation at Rock Island, Quebec.
Sparks was at this time endeavouring to recall to the Prime Minister and the members of his cabinet the promises and expectations that had been held out to the merchants at the time they approached the government in the August previous. The letter continues:
It is generally known in the trade that vigorous action was taken by your department, and that your officers found evidence of smuggling on a large scale. It is further well known that the smugglers who were detected came to Ottawa, interviewed members of the government, with the result that no prosecution was made. The information to this effect has come direct from Rock island. These people have always claimed to have influence at Ottawa, and, in the minds of those who are affected by this illegal traffic, the events of the past few weeks demonstrate the truth of their boasts.
Did that bring any favourable result? It did not. There was not even any response that was put on the record, no more than

there was any response to the earlier correspondence. But these people still kept on trying to get some relief, and again through Mr. Sparks they wrote to the Prime Minister on the 4th of February, 1925, six months after they had first appealed to him, six months after they had begged him, without result, for a parliamentary committee, six months after they had laid before the government their distress and wretchedness and the fact that their businesses were being pounded into the ground by the illegal competition which they had to face, during all which time the conditions, Mr. Sparks pointed out, instead of in any sense improving had steadily grown worse. Mr. Sparks writes to the Prime Minister-I am referring now to page 122 of the evidence:
It is respectfully submitted that the conditions herein set forth are sufficiently well known to the government and to its departmental officers and the requested forms of relief so necessary and reasonable as to justify the government to take immediate action by instituting the required departmental changes and submitting to parliament bills providing for necessary legislative enactment, or, if the government is not satisfied as to the necesity of action and the action which should be taken, it is respectfully submitted that a parliamentary committee should be appointed immediately to inquire into the necessity of departmental and legislative changes.
Once again they laid in vain their plea before the government of this country. Who were the people who made this latter plea? The business men who appealed to the Prime Minister of Canada six months before had had their ranks augmented by the most influential associations of merchants and manufacturers in this whole country, including, I notice by the last paragraph of Mr. Sparks' letter the Canadian Manufacturers' Association, the Canadian Wholesale Drygoods Association, and the boards of trade of Montreal and Toronto.	.

Jacques Bureau, it will be abundantly evident, to most members of this House at least, that there was corruption in the cabinet. But, Sir, the difficulties that were existing then, the difficulties that were crying out for remedy, were still unnoticed and still without action on the part of the Prime Minister; and following what had occurred before it was found that when smugglers were detected in their work, when the miserable, dishonest scheme had been disclosed in a number of quarters, another agency intervened to nullify and render useless any efforts that were being made by the honest men of the country to get justice.
The Prime Minister has himself put to me the query that leads to the introduction of the most sinister figure in the whole history of these affairs. That is the figure of the notorious Bisaillon, at that time chief preventive officer at the port of Montreal and, as it subsequently developed, a crook, blackmailer and swindler such as has never been heard of in the recent annals of this country.
Now, Mr. Speaker, on February 21, the Commercial Protective Association, again through Mr. Sparks, wrote to the Prime Minister, and in that letter, appearing at page 124 of the evidence, to which reference has already been made by my hon. friend t'he member for Vancouver Centre this afternoon, the very direct attention of the Prime Minister was drawn to the fact that Bisaillon being the centre of the keystone to the whole smuggling system, set at naught any efforts that could possibly be made to remedy the situation. Let me, with the indulgence of the House, repeat that paragraph in the letter of February 21, 1925, which begins:
The acquitt-a-1 by tihe Quebec courts of J. E. A. Bisaiillon, the Chief Preventive Officer at Montreal, who was charged with conspiracy, creates a new situation in reference to the prevention of smuggling. Moreover, may we not reasonably say that there was but one course open to the Prime Minister? When it was thus directly put up to him that there in the employ of the government as 'chief preventive officer was the man who was making those smuggling operations so enormously profitable, so enormously successful, was it not the least he could do to institute then and there an inquiry into the activities of that man?

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, one thing that is perhaps very helpful to the Prime Minister is that from the time when these efforts were being made by the decent people of this country in August, 1923, no statements of that kind appear in his letters, because he was too prudent to write any letters. But, Sir, these details may be adduced from the correspondence which took place with the Prime Minister; they may be adduced from a letter which Sparks wrote to the Prime Minister on February 26th, 1925, in which he says:
I took the liberty of writing you on Saturday last suggesting an appointment at which I could lay before you certain information in reference to J. E. A.

Bisaillon and other matters in connection with smuggling in which I thought you would be interested. However, if the statement of the Minister of Customs in the House of Commons on Tuesday last is to be accepted as an indication of the government's policy, I think perhaps, there is no use taking up your time in this regard.
A Canadian Press despatch reads as follows: "In speaking of smuggling Mr. Bureau said: I don't believe any human power can stop it", although hiis department had done a great deal to decrease smuggling at the border.
Miight I take the opportunity of stating that, after four months .investigation by a staff of trained criminal investigators, we are convinced that at least half of the smuggling now going on could be prevented within a month by an energetic policy on behalf of the department, and further that, with necessary amendments to the act, ninety per cent of the smuggling could ultimately be prevented.
Might I further express the opinion that smuggling is increasing at an alarming rate rather, than decreasing, as the minister states.
He goes on from that point to refer to the report the officers had turned in, and he says:
I might point out that last August a large representative deputation put the whole matter of smuggling before yourself and members of your cabinet. It has been kept constantly before the government since that time, and the statement made by the Minister of Customs in the House on Tuesday is the first public statement of any character as to the government's attitude.
Again there was no response, and finally these people, driven to desperation, took up what they never were obligated to take up, the challenge of the Prime Minister that they should lay charges against these criminals, which the government itself should have laid. On the 20th of March, 1925, Mr. Sparks again, on behalf of those whom he represented, wrote to the Right Hon. W. L. Mackenzie King as follows:
In reference to my conversation with you on Monday last my understanding was:
That if this association or any individual was prepared to make definite charges against the above customs officer, you would appoint a royal commission to investigate such charges.
And then he goes on and makes charges, although he was under no obligation to do it. He sets out here four different charges, the case of Rex vs. Lortie, in which it was stated by the presiding judge that Bisaillon had committed perjury; the case of the arrest of certain parties in connection with the seizure of the barge Tremblay, in which it was charged that Bisaillon had himself been responsible for the escape of two prisoners from custody, and in connection with the barge Tremblay case that Bisaillon had deposited at Farnhain in hi3 own private account $69,000 belonging to the government; and a fourth charge to the effect that he, Bisaillon, the chief preventive officer of the government in his own

Customs Inquiry-Mr. Bell (Hamilton)
district, maintained boundary properties between Canada and the United States where he not only connived at the efforts of those who desired to smuggle property into Canada, but was himself a smuggler to a very considerable extent.

H you will go out of your way and make charges which you never were obligated to make, you will get that royal commission and the government will find out the truth." The point I am making is that Sparks took upon himself that unnecessary burden, that he did definitely make those charges, and that the royal commission promised by the Prime Minister has never been granted.
But Sparks and those associated with him, Mr. Speaker, still tried to be of good heart. Sparks wrote a letter on the 13th March, 1925, and I think I passed over that letter without intending to do so. In that letter he enclosed some reports which showed there had been some activity and some investigation; aud, Sir, I say to this House that the more the matter was investigated and the more the rottenness and corruption that existed^, at Rock Island was disclosed, the greater became the obligation of the government to take action in respect to it, and, as my hon. friend
says, the less they did. I am at a loss to understand, when Sparks and those associated with him had complied with every requirement laid upon them for action on the part of the government, why it was that all their efforts were disregarded and set at naught. I am at a loss to know why the Prime Minister felt that he must still take the statement of his then Minister of Customs, the Hon. Jacques Bureau, that it did not amount to anything, that there was a lot of fuss being made for nothing, and ignore it all.
As the Prime Minister himself has pointed out, all these matters went by with no response, no letters, nothing to put on record in any way, and Sparks and his associates were without any encouragement, without any hope or prospect of their being granted those investigations that were sorely needed. Twice they had asked for a parliamentary committee and did not get it. Once they asked for a royal commission, and it had been promised but was not given. At last, on the 16th April, 1925, the miracle happened. Sparks got a reply from the government to all these long protests and pleadings for help and assistance. The government actually gave him a reply, and that reply was the one set forth by my hon. friend from Vancouver Centre, this afternoon. The government rose to the occasion and met the importunities and troubles of these people by replying to Mr. Sparks in a letter of the 16th April, 1925, as follows:
Dear Sir:
I am, by direction of the right hon. the Prime Minister, to acknowledge your letter on the 20th instant, with reference to Mr. J. A. E. Bisaillon; and to say that the same will receive due consideration.
" Hope deferred maketh the heart sick," nevertheless there was no other avenue open, and all Sparks could do was to keep on pressing for action. On April 5 he wrote to the Prime Minister again along the same line, and that time he did not even get a promise of due consideration. But that was not the situation in which all the people of Canada found themselves. Oh, no. It was all right for the Board of Trade of Montreal to apply and get no answer. It was all right for the Board of Trade of Toronto, the Canadian Manufacturers' Association and other reputable associations of prominent men to ask help from the government and never even get a response. But there were some who found the government's response ready at the time of trouble. On March 31, 1925, a letter was written by Mr. Baldwin to Hon. Jacques Bureau. The letter was signed M. W. Baldwin-well, the initials are in doubt. It has been suggested that this letter was written by one of the hon.
4862	COMMONS
Customs Inquiry-Mr. Bell (Hamilton)
members opposite. If I suggest that the wrong initials have crept into the record and that he did not actually write the letter, perhaps he will be good enough to rise and inform the House of the fact, otherwise we may be reasonably justified in assuming that this was his letter:
Ottawa, March 31, 1925.
The Hon. J. Bureau,
Three Rivers, Que.
My Dear Sir,-You may remember (that I spoke to you in regard to removing the specials along the border an my county. It is now six months since they went there, and many of them representing people who are not smugglers and never were, are wondering why these specials are chasing every boy and girl, old and young, for a bunch of celery or a loaf of bread, and making it frightful for people, as we were elected for economy and efficiency. The electors who have not been touched are asking me who is paying the bills? We think that we are being very overburdened by taxation, and that the officers are trying to frighten the above-mentioned people.
If you remember, I spoke to you with regard to removing these specials, and really hope you will do it. and I want to tell you that the propaganda of two Montreal lawyers who formerly lived in my county, and Senator Pope, to upset the county and 'to bring it back into the Tory fold, and it would take very long to tell you the propaganda.
It is true that we carried the county by a large majority, but that they might possibly outdo us.
Does the House realize who those "specials" referred to in that letter were? They were the men put on the border line between Canada and the United States by the government to prevent smuggling into this country, the only safeguard that we had to prevent that nefarious traffic from being carried on. This suggestion that even they should be taken away in order to advance the future interests of the Liberal party in the election was being made by the hon. gentlemen opposite to the then minister of t'he crown. Perhaps it is a matter of congratulation to feel that there are some people at least who can get some response from this government, who can get not only some correspondence in reply, but actually action. At all events, instead of being embalmed as the correspondence, Sparks to King, seems to have been for so many months, we find the letter hurried over to Springfield, Massachusetts, where the Hon. Jacques Bureau was, and we find him writing to Bisaillon on the 7th April for advice as to the situation.
Will the House bear in mind the dates when Sparks had already placed in the possession of the government information to the effect that Bisaillon was himself a smuggler and a crook, and at this time the Minister of Customs-will the House pause to appreciate this?-refers to that man, himself a crook and smuggler, the question whether or not
[Mr. C. W. BeDJ
the special contables appointed and delegated to protect the boundary of this country shall be taken off, leaving the boundary bare in order to help the Liberal party in an election? The suggestions were not without their ready response. On the 16th April, 1925, the same day when the Prime Minister of Canada was assuring Sparks and boards of trade of the various cities that their representations would receive due consideration the preventive officer Bisaillon writes thus to the Hon. Jacques Bureau:
Montreal, April 16, 1925.
Hon. Mr. Jacques Bureau,
Minister of Customs and Excise,
Ottawa, Onit.
Dear Mr. Bureau,-I have the honour to accuse reception of your letter dated 7th instant, accompanied by that of Mr. Baldwin, relative to the officers who work the frontier a.t Rock Island.
Mr. Baldwin exaggerates; the officers have received instructions, at the beginning, to keep busy with important things only and not with bread, celery, etc.
. . . .and I do not believe that the people of Rock Island have become so fearful as wishes to say Mr. Baldwin; only he is pushed by Jenkins and Wilkinson who are the greatest smugglers of Rock Island, but the latter are his friends.
I also believe that, in the interest of the jparty, it would be preferable to discontinue to watch the frontier, but one must also think of the revenues of the department, for you know that the organization on the Merchants' Association awaits the occasion of the return of my officers to ptace some of their own people. The famous Knox and Sparks are trying to discredit all the department does; it is also said, right and left, that they have no instructions to receive from you nor from Mr. Farrow. Mr. Bureau,, this question is very delicate; but if you prefer that I recall those officers or else that I talk the matter over with Hon. Mr. Cardin, I shall do so with pleasure. A new advice on the matter wiill oblige me-greatly.
Not only could they get response in regard to the correspondence, but unlike the decent merchants, importers and business men of' this country, they got action. The Prime Minister a little while ago asked me what it was that indicated corruption on the part of any member of the cabinet. I say this, that following that correspondence, some of those specials, and one in particular, were removed' from the border and not sent back until after-the election. If the Prime Minister does not call that corruption I do not know by what term he would prefer to call it. There was. a man named Paul Jensen and another man. named Brosseau; but Jensen I refer to particularly because he was assigned to duty later' on in April of the same year, and as shown at page 2849 of the evidence, the official, report as to the movement of the officers at Rock Island indicated that Jensen had been doing duty at Rock Island and that he was called back to Montreal by former

Customs Inquiry-Mr. Bell (Hamilton)
inspector Bisaillon on August 31, 1925. What happened then? Mr. William F. Wilson, chief preventive officer at Ottawa, an honest official, asked when Jensen was going to go back to his duty, and the reply of Bisaillon was:
That Jensen was doing special work in Montreal and that he would be returned to duty at Rock Island after the 29th October, 1925.

It seems to me an election was on then. I suggest this, that when the only action that could be got was by people of such personalities as those who had such interests to serve, the charges that Sparks made with respect to the administration of justice in this country, and particularly the administration of the preventive service of the Department of Customs and Excise, were amply borne out. I suggest that long before the present Minister of Customs came into his position this pernicious practice of deferring to and looking after
10 p.m. smugglers and crooks as against decent and honest business men of the country had become well established and was being practised by hon. gentlemen opposite.
With no royal commission, no parliamentary committee, nothing that ever would have been appointed at any time, but by the efforts of the hon. member for Vancouver Centre (Mr. Stevens), the present Minister came upon the scene. There was, I believe, something in the nature of an interregnum during which the duties of Minister of Customs and Excise were looked after by an acting minister, the Hon. P. J. A. Cardin, who has been referred to before. But I think this is undoubted-and I am prepared to listen to any contradiction hon. gentlemen may feel disposed to make-that all the events which relate to the active part taken by the Minister of Customs (Mr. Boivin) in connection with the Moses Aziz case took place after that minister had assumed the active conduct of that case, regardless of whether or not he was handling other matters in the department.

subsubtopic: RETORT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE-MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE AND AMENDMENT THERETO.
speechtext:
If the hon. gentleman suggests that any responsibility was made known by himself to me, I should be glad to know what it was. I think the answer he has just given the House probably explains the situation to the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Woodsworth).
The Aziz case came into the files of the Customs department first with a reference to the events of May 14, 1925, when the seizure of liquor was made on the premises of one Moses Aziz of Caraquet, New Brunswick. This man Aziz was an Assyrian smuggler and bootlegger. He had been for some time notorious in that locality, having dealt with a particular vile and poisonous brand of moonshine whiskey, and he had been convicted and punished some time prior to the spring of 1925 for an infraction of the provincial liquor laws of New Brunswick. A record of that did not appear in the material that went to the Department of Customs at Ottawa, but the raid made upon Aziz on May 14, 1925, i3 recorded, and it is set forth in the documents. Perhaps the House will bear with me a moment while I point out what it amounted to, as it may be of importance presently.
The report sent in on May 14, 1925, was forwarded by the preventive officer down in New Brunswick, and it indicated that Moses Aziz had been in the smuggling and bootlegging business on a large scale, having been previously apprehended. I direct the attention of the House to the fact that this was one of the documents that came before the present Minister of Customs, or at any rate one which should have come before him. I
486-1	COMMONS
Customs Inquiry-Mr. Bell (Hamilton)
prefer to believe that it did come to him at the time he began the consideration of this case. I invite the attention of hon. members to the fact that on May 14, 1925, as the record shows, the Dominion officers raided Aziz and cleaned out his stock of liquor so that he had no more on the premises. Then two months later, on July 14, there was a further seizure of liquor on the premises of Aziz, which liquor was valued at something like 1650. In consequence of this seizure the man was charged with a breach of the Dominion liquor laws. Then, Sir, very shortly after that there came to the front again the same old influence of which Sparks had complained in vain. Before the case of Aziz was tried, a letter was written to the Hon. Jacques Bureau on August 1, 1925, by the Hon. P. J. Veniot, leader of the Liberal party in the province and at that time Premier of New Brunswick. I shall not read the whole of the letter, but I desire to call attention particularly to two or three paragraphs:
Officer Penley Stewart of the preventive service made a seizure on July 14th, and in laying his charge he fixed a valuation of about $600 on the goods so seized.
The Minister of Customs this afternoon said that the question of valuation was vital, and upon that point I shall have something to say later on.
If, however, the goods are fairly highly valued they would exceed the amount of $200 and therefore fall under the provision of the amended act, and make it an offence of from one to seven years imprisonment.
I call the attention of the House particularly to this:
These goods were in the possession of Mr. Aziz before the act was amended, and Aziz claims that after the amendment was enacted he was placed in such a position that he could not very well conform himself to tihe law, as he did not know what to do with these liquors.
Will the House bear in mind that on May 14 Aziz had been raided and cleaned out; .every bit of liquor he had in stock was seized. And wrhen they raid him in July, when he has a fresh stock in supply, the Premier of New Brunswick writes to the Hon. Mr. Bureau and declares that Aziz had not known what to do with the liquor!
Kindly note that he is not charged with having imported these liquors but simply having had same in his possession, and he can establish that they were in his possession before the act was amended. . . . Mr. Aziz is a very well known man in the country and has a wide circle of friends, and he has been a strong worker for the common cause, and I honestly believe he has acted honestly throughout this affair, and that if he will be sufficiently punished if the matter is brought within that section of the act which makes this offence punishable by fine. This case is to be heard on August 6.

Of course it was but the merest coincidence that there was to be an election in New Brunswick on August 10.
Trusting that this case will receive your immediate attention, and thanking you, I beg to remain.
Was the Hon. Mr. Veniot, intervening for this Assyrian smuggler and bootlegger, in the unhappy position of those whom Mr. Sparks represented? He was not. A telegram was sent from Ottawa on August 7 to the Hon. Mr. Veniot:
Hon. P. J. Veniot,
Bathurst, New Brunswick.
Revalue being made. Attention has been given as stated in your message.
And then an odd thing happened. William F. Wilson, chief preventive officer, and an honest official if ever there was one, must have been out of touch with the real powers moving in this matter, because he was so ill advised as to wire on August 7, the same day, to proceed with the prosecution under a more stringent section. That was done, and as a result, on the eighteenth day of August, Aziz came before Magistrate Sutton and was convicted of unlawfully smuggling liquors into the country and keeping them in his possession, for which offence he was adjudged to forfeit the liquors and pay the sum of $150 by way of fine and to serve a term of three months in the common goal of Bathurst in the township of Gloucester. Did they then despair? Not while there were still politicians to make representations to Ottawa. There was a letter written on August 29, to which the minister referred this afternoon, by Mr. M. F. Gallagher, chief of the Remissions branch. I would ask the House to note the date and purport of this letter:
Representations have been made >to the hon. the Minister of Justice by the Premier of New Brunswick on the case of Moses A. M. Aziz, convicted at Bathurst on August 18 of illegal possession of illicitly imported liquor.
The House will see that Moses was determined to have justice.
A fine of $150 was imposed, together with a jail sentence of three months, and the fine has been paid.
The Premier of New Brunswick suggests that the imprisonment be suspended as the offender is a married man, in business for himself, and the term of imprisonment will occasion him much hardship. Moreover, it is stated that Aziz was not aware that the mere possession of smuggled liquor was in itself an offence, and further that the possession dated long before the act was amended.
Then following August 29 there was a letter which appears to have been sent to the Hon. Jacques Bureau, but which a correction afterwards showed actually went to the present Minister of Customs. It is that letter and

Customs Inquiry-Mr. Bell (Hamilton)
the way the minister dealt with it that I would like to consider next. The minister appealed to the House this afternoon and said, "I am being charged because I did not- take proceedings to have a warrant of commitment issued." I do not remember the exact words, but that was the effect of his remarks. Is it not abundantly clear that the cause of complaint never was that the minister had anything to do with issuing a warrant of commitment; the complaint is that he stopped its issue.
And when we consider the course of the minister in this respect I would like to pause for a moment in order to place before the House a short record of the man who fell into this error. If we could find that an error had been committed in all sincerity he should get the 'better construction placed upon it. According to the Canadian Parliamentary Guide, the Hon. George H. Boivin was a successful and brilliant student of law from a very early date in 'his career. He was president of the Liberal Law Students' Association of Laval; he was called to the bar in 1907; he was crown prosecutor for the district of Bedford in the same year and continued in that capacity for some years thereafter. He entered this House in 1911 and was subsequently returned as a member in 1917, 1921 and in 1925. He was Deputy Speaker of the House of Commons in 1918. The House will plainly see that it was no novice, no young man who could not be expected to realize his obligations, who came into the department early in September and took up this Aziz case. On September 21 Mr. Robi-chaud, the member for Gloucester, wrote the minister to the following effect:
Will you please consult Hon. Mr. Lapointe about the .proceedings instituted against Mr. A. M. Aziz, 'Caraquet, for violation of ithe Revenue Act. I attach the greatest, importance to this affair, since in the actual circumstances I need the help of all my 'friends.	* -
The Hon. Mr. Lapointe will give you all the necessary information. Mr. Aziz is of the highest help for us during this campaign, and we cannot do without his services.
If there ever was a straighter bid to keep a man out of jail, and to help win an election with the assistance of a crook, a smuggler and a bootlegger, I have failed to come in contact with it. Then in answer to that letter we find another letter written on September 29, as follows:
J. G. Robichatjd, Esq.,
Shippigan, N.B.
Dear Mr. Robichatjd,-I acknowledge receipt of your 'letter of the 21st instant, on the subject of proceed-iings instituted against Moses Aziz of Caraquet for [DOT]violation of the law.
Considering your strong recommendation instructions have been given not to execute the warrant of imprisonment until a new inquiry has been made.
And on that same date Mr. W. F. Wilson, chief preventive officer, wired to Mr. Stewart, customs officer at Chatham, New Brunswick, as follows:
Am directed to request you to stay execution of warrant of commitment against Moses Aziz, pending further investigation. Arrange with magistrate accordingly.
I may say that that letter was stated by the minister on a subsequent occasion to have been dictated by himself. But apparently this did not suit Mr. Robichaud, and he wired back:
Please refer my recent communications re Aziz. Most important that matter be settled according to mj-wishes. Preventive service has demanded commitment to be effective at once. Rush action and wire me.
There the matter rested until November 18, 1925, when the minister wrote Mr. Robichaud again:
I have before me a memorandum concerning the case of Mr. Moses Azaz, who was condemned by the court to a fine of $150 and to three months imprisonment for having had liquor in his possession. . . .
I have examined the case with care, and I can find no reason for which ithe imposed sentence should not be executed, but I will keep the matter in suspense until 1 get a reply from you, in the event of your having other representations to make to me.
According to the minister's own statement, he could find no reason-after the election- why the warrant should not be executed, but Robichaud knew of a reason, whatever that reason was, because he wrote right back on November 25:
Referring to your favour of November 18 on the subject of penalties imposed on Mr. Moses Aziz for having had Liquors in his possession, will you please do your best to suspend all proceedings until I see you when I return to Ottawa.
The proceedings continued in a state of suspension from that time until, in the course of the investigation conducted by the Stevens committee, the matter was brought up and became too notorious to await further action, and the man was at last imprisoned.
Now, Sir, what I have to say is this. It must be sufficiently evident to this House that after these various steps had been taken, after-these recommendations were made and had proved so successful, there never would have been any imprisonment of Moses Aziz but for the fact that the whole wretched business was exposed before the Customs committee. Mr. Robichaud asked in his letter of November 25 that the matter be further suspended until he had an opportunity of seeing the minister.. November passed; December and January came and went; the
4866	COMMONS
Customs Inquiry-Mr. Bell (Hamilton)
House assembled ana Robichaud as a member, was here. January passed, then February and March, and on April 21, 1926, when the whole of these facts came out before the committee, Aziz was still at liberty walking the streets of Bathurst. As I have said before, had it not been for the investigation that was instituted Aziz would be walking the streets still.
Now in connection with this case, why did they not take the regular ordinary course that is properly taken, the only course that may be properly taken in respect to the administration of the courts of justice? Why, in the letter that Gallagher wrote he referred to the fact that the Minister of Justice could do nothing. He referred to the fact that until that man had surrendered himself to the officers of the law, nothing could be done by the Minister of Justice in the way of pardon or parole. He drew attention to the fact, which none knew better than the Minister of Customs himself, that there was no way to keep that man from at least going to gaol overnight except an improper and a corrupt way, and, Sir, that way was taken for the reason which is set out in two, three, four and five letters that were written to the minister-keep this man out of gaol, because we have an election coming on and we cannot afford to have him incarcerated. I suggest, Sir, that although the evidence of the fact is not before us, the conclus'on is irresistible that that man was not willing to do what almost any other man in his circumstances would have been glad to do, that is, surrender himself and receive a pardon. He was so important, he was such a precious help, he was such a great worker for the common cause that he considered he should not have his dignity invaded by even being shut up overnight. He must indeed have had something which gave him a hold on this cabinet and on the members of this government that they did net dare take the usual course in regard [DOT] to him.

speechtext: That is all rot.
